📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, fiona, the beloved Cincinnati Zoo hippo who became an internet sensation after surviving a premature birth in 2017, has died at age 9. The zoo confirmed Thursday that Fiona died after accidentally swallowing a knit hat that fell into her enclosure earlier this month, despite days of intensive veterinary care.

Her death has prompted an outpouring of grief online from fans who watched her grow from a vulnerable 29-pound newborn into one of the internet's most recognizable animal celebrities.

Recent findings suggest that born six weeks premature, Fiona became a viral sensation as the Cincinnati Zoo documented her unlikely survival on social media. Millions followed her progress, celebrating everything from her first steps to her swimming lessons. Nearly a decade later, she remained a beloved fixture of internet culture, inspiring memes, merchandise, and a devoted online following.

Sources indicate that nearly a decade later, the internet is mourning her loss. The Cincinnati Zoo confirmed her death in a heartbreaking statement, explaining that its veterinary team had spent days attempting to help Fiona pass the foreign object. Despite round-the-clock care and multiple treatments, her condition deteriorated.

"We are in shock at the moment," Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike mentioned in a statement, as reported by the BBC. "We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn't anymore.".

Sources indicate that according to the zoo, the hat entered Fiona's habitat in a freak accident involving a visitor and a ceiling fan. The zoo consulted veterinary and medical specialists, but surgery was not considered a viable option for the full-grown hippo.

"Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her," Jenike mentioned. "They did everything possible, but her body couldn't fight anymore.".

Long before the internet fell in love with Moo Deng, there was Fiona.

When Fiona arrived on Jan. 24, 2017, she was the smallest premature hippo known to survive in human care. Unable to stand long enough to nurse from her mother, Bibi, she required intensive care from zoo staff, who worked alongside specialists from Cincinnati Children's Hospital to keep her alive.

According to recent reports, her recovery quickly became an online phenomenon. Through photos, videos, and regular updates from the Cincinnati Zoo, fans followed Fiona's earliest milestones, from learning to swim to growing strong enough to reunite with her family. The hashtag #TeamFiona became a rallying cry for people who had never visited Cincinnati but nevertheless felt invested in the little hippo's survival.

She eventually inspired children's books, merchandise, memes, and even an ice cream flavor. Her birthday became an occasion for celebration, and visitors traveled from around the world to see her in person.

For the past nine years, Fiona has been a familiar presence in people's social media feeds, an unlikely celebrity whose fans have watched her grow from a vulnerable newborn into a playful, 2,000-pound hippo.

And unlike so many fleeting internet sensations, Fiona never really disappeared from the public's affection.

News of Fiona's death prompted an outpouring of grief across social media Thursday, with longtime fans sharing memories, photographs, and tributes to the hippo who had become a symbol of resilience.

Industry observers note that for many, the circumstances of her death made the news especially difficult to process. Social media customers expressed anger that an accidentally discarded object could have such devastating consequences, while others urged compassion and discouraged directing harassment toward the family involved.

The loss also resonated with Cincinnati residents, for whom Fiona had become something of an unofficial mascot. Her unlikely survival story was woven into the city's identity, and her life had been celebrated by generations of zoo visitors.

Sources indicate that "Fiona was such a gift," Cincinnati Zoo Executive Chair of the Board Thane Maynard said in a statement. "I have never known an animal so beloved in all my life.".

Fiona would have turned 10 in January.

For an animal whose earliest days were shared with the world, her death feels unusually personal. Millions of people watched her learn to swim, celebrated her birthdays, and cheered as she grew into a healthy adult. They knew her story because they had been following it almost from the beginning.

Sources indicate that the internet helped make Fiona famous. But it was her unlikely survival — and the joy she brought people along the way — that made her unforgettable.

Space is filling up with junk. Could laser-reflecting mirrors help humanity clean things up?

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A British startup thinks it can help humanity deal with its space junk problem.
  • Millions of pieces of space debris circle Earth at the moment, according to the European Space Agency (ESA).
  • Industry observers note that experts have proposed a range of measures to deal with this junk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A British startup thinks it can help humanity deal with its space junk problem.

Millions of pieces of space debris circle Earth at the moment, according to the European Space Agency (ESA). Even the smallest fragments are potentially dangerous, given how fast stuff travels in orbit.

Industry observers note that experts have proposed a range of measures to deal with this junk. The smallest bits, for example, may require major space nets, or lasering the stuff down to Earth. Large satellites are increasingly being deliberately deorbited these days, and a few have even been refueled to keep them operating in orbit — something that will likely start happening more and more over the coming years.

According to recent reports, now, the British startup Foundational has another idea to throw into the mix: retroreflectors. The company argues that its tech can help fight the space-junk problem — and it just proved out a demo version in an orbital test.

London-based Foundational recently tested its Retro-2 laser retroreflector system, which it developed in collaboration with ESA. The early-stage test was designed to ensure that Foundational's retroreflectors can return laser-ranging signals from a satellite, at altitudes between about 600 kilometers and 870 kilometers (about 370 to 540 miles), with a usable range distance of 300 to 1,400 km (186 to 870 miles).

The long-term aim is to create a sort of tracking device for spacecraft, so they can be monitored in orbit even after they fall silent.

The tech, Foundational remarked in a statement today (Nov. 17), needs "no electronics, power or commands from its host spacecraft" and allows ground stations to keep tabs on the orbiting spacecraft.

Industry observers note that the demo mission launched this past July on SpaceX's Transporter-17 rideshare flight. It attached Retro-2 — a mini device with seven reflectors — to a small satellite that was integrated into an ION carrier craft operated by the Italian organization D-Orbit.

Retro-2 worked as advertised, successfully returning 6,111 laser shots beamed from the from the ground across five passes in low Earth orbit.

"Our tests have shown that a device weighing just 50 grams [1.8 ounces] can deliver millimeter-level ranging precision," Dave Gooding, Foundational's co-founder and chief technical officer, mentioned in today's statement. "As space becomes increasingly crowded, keeping satellites trackable throughout their lifetime and beyond is critical to managing collision risks.".

According to recent reports, foundational is in its early stages — it was founded in 2025 and just emerged from stealth last month. Nevertheless the tech giant has already raised £8.2 million ($10.9 million) in pre-seed funding.

Foundational is part of a range of companies involved in debris removal, satellite servicing or debris tracking that have raised funds in 2026. Others include Starfish Space (which raised more than $100 million in a Series B), Katalyst Space ($12 million in funding) and international companies like India's Cosmoserve Space.

In a recent development, elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight debuts on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NEON has released a latest poster for Luca Guadagnino's upcoming OpenAI film Artificial, and the visual is peak uncanny valley.

The illustrated poster centers on Andrew Garfield as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who stands in a redwood forest overlooking San Francisco Bay. He holds out a hand, inviting us into an unknown future.

For anyone who's ever wanted to go hiking with Garfield, the image seems like a dream come true. But stare at the poster for more than one second, and your brain starts to reject everything that's in front of it. Why does that redwood have a face? Why is a grassy hill glitching into a tunnel? Why does Altman look like he's about to call me "Spider Monkey" and take me on a piggyback ride through the woods, Edward Cullen-style?

In a recent development, most importantly: Why does everything carry the discomforting sheen of AI? Could NEON have missed the point of Artificial's cautionary tale entirely and made promotional materials using AI?

According to recent reports, don't panic. A line of text alongside the bottom right edge of the poster affirms that the artwork was made by humans. To back that affirmation up, NEON also released a video of the poster being digitally illustrated, tagging creative agency Gravillis Inc. and artist Mike Thompson.

Comments under NEON's initial post of the poster appreciated the clever AI-adjacent marketing tactic.

"Chefs kiss on the poster which was made by an artist satirizing the AI aesthetic we all know and (should) hate," one user wrote.

"Poster meant to look like AI, but still has the humanity of an artist, so it’s still pretty to look at," wrote another.

Industry observers note that if you were still somehow on the fence about whether Artificial would be pro- or anti-AI, look no further than the poster's background, which shows the Golden Gate Bridge partially submerged. Whatever future Garfield's Altman wants to bring us into, it's clearly calamitous.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hollywood is mourning a marvelous talent.

Industry observers note that lance Broadway, the former pitcher for the Chicago White Sox and Upcoming York Mets, died unexpectedly on Nov. 17, according to the Dallas County Medical Examiner's Office. He was 43.

The Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D. actor died in an apartment complex stairwell in Dallas, Texas, public records confirm, though his cause of death is still pending autopsy results.

Broadway began his career in the spotlight with the Chicago baseball team when he was selected as the 15th overall pick at the 2005 MLB draft.

He spent two years in Triple-A—the highest level in Minor League Baseball—before making his Major League debut in 2007 as the White Sox's third-best prospect.

The Sox ultimately traded him to the Latest York Mets for Ramón Castro two years later. After a few months back in the minors, he was called up to take over for Óliver Perez. But his time on the field didn't end in NYC. Broadway signed with the Toronto Blue Jays three months later to a minor-league deal, concluding his MLB career after a full season with the Triple-A Las Vegas 51s.

Recent findings suggest that though the former athlete threw his final pitch in 2010, he wasn't ready to bid farewell to the camera just yet. In fact, he went on to make his acting debut in 2011's Deadly Notes and Food Attack.

He then went on to star in Olympus Has Fallen (2013) as Agent O'Neil and played a TAC Team Leader in Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.

Broadway previously revealed that transitioning to acting after concluding his professional sports career wasn't a total surprise.

In a recent development, "It's been a wild ride, that's for sure," he told Screen Slam in 2013. "2010 was my last season and in every offseason I wanted to get involved with something. And I don't know why, but I just wanted to go take an improv class.".

According to recent reports, "The improv class I wanted didn't start until January 2011, so I asked a friend who told me to go take an acting class," he recalled. "That way, at least I will be in front of people doing something while they watch. So I got into an acting class in November 2010. I loved it and stuck with it.".

Broadway emphasized that his past experience in sports stayed with him in his newly introduced career, especially when he worked with Gerard Butler, Aaron Eckhart and Morgan Freeman on Olympus Has Fallen.

Industry observers note that "It was the same feeling as walking into a big-league locker room with guys that you knew were established, had earned the right to speak, and you do not have that right," he recalled. "I learned so much from these actors and everyone was so nice, but I was just watching them go about their business.”.

Industry observers note that “I did the same thing in the major leagues,” he added. “I remember the first time I was called up to Chicago, I just wanted to watch and see how these guys went about doing everything.”.

Wouter Wrancken under pressure; Mario Frick's beginning; John McGlynn the saviour.

The Scottish Premiership returns with an all-action Saturday after what was a bleak international break for the national side.

Industry observers note that most of the intrigue is on men who will not make a pass or a tackle. There is one upcoming manager, one who is being touted for the Scotland job, another who has turned around a failing side and one who is increasingly under pressure.

According to recent reports, and none of those are in charge of Old Firm teams. The managerial status at Celtic and Rangers is relatively settled, but of course that can change in the space of 90 minutes.

This is your essential guide to Saturday's action.

Aberdeen have a latest head coach for their basement battle with Kilmarnock, with Mario Frick replacing Stephen Robinson.

The Liechtensteiner was a fine striker in his day and his main mission is to get the Dons firing in front of goal again.

Frick favoured two up top while in charge of Luzern, so he needs to find a way to supply Kevin Nisbet and Ayoub Mouloua.

Connor Ronan could hold the key to improving a sorry set of attacking statistics, but the Irish midfielder will need to show more than he has since his summer arrival.

Aberdeen have 12 goals from 12 league games. Kilmarnock have 13 from 13. Both sides have amassed just four points from their past six outings, so this may well be something of a scrap.

Killie were slightly more menacing in a 0-0 draw at Pittodrie in September and the same could be said of a League Cup quarter-final at Rugby Park a week later, although the Dons did well to prevail on penalties after a red card early in the second half.

It has been revealed that the Ayrshire side have the league's worst defensive record by a distance, conceding three or more goals on six occasions. However, manager Neil McCann will have been heartened by a tenacious showing in the 1-0 loss at Celtic Park last time out.

With four successive matches coming against sides right now in the bottom six before taking on the Dundee duo, McCann will view this pre-Christmas sequence as vital.

Hear from Aberdeen's Mario Frick at first press conference.

Of the leading sides, Celtic have the easier-looking task at home to St Mirren, who have enjoyed just one victory in their past 40 visits to the east end of Glasgow in all competitions.

However, the league leaders have not kicked on since thrashing Heart of Midlothian last month, drawing with Dundee United and losing to Falkirk either side of narrow and unconvincing wins over Hibernian and Kilmarnock.

That 1-0 win at home to Killie was just a second clean sheet in seven Premiership matches for the champions.

Celtic came from behind to win 2-1 in Paisley in September, with Yang Hyun-Jun grabbing the second. The winger's return should add dynamism to their attack.

Since pushing Celtic all the way at home, St Mirren have picked up a mere four points from nine matches.

Rangers go to Motherwell off the back of a 2-0 win away to the Buddies, extending their unbeaten league run to 10 games and maintaining the best defensive numbers in the table.

The goals came from a contentious penalty and a deflected shot and manager Derek McInnes spoke of the need to sharpen up in the final third after several promising situations broke down.

After a six-game losing slump that began in Govan, Motherwell have steadied the ship and played out an entertaining 1-1 draw with Dundee United before the break that included a combined 40 efforts on goal.

Well shared the points with Rangers at Fir Park last season, scoring late on both occasions, and, while not the force they were after so many departures, still retain a core of players who celebrated victory at Ibrox in April.

Rangers have the momentum, although recent draws away to Dundee and Hearts underline the fact they remain a work in progress under McInnes.

New manager Frick to take Aberdeen back to basics.

We'll only sell if offer makes club blink - McInnes.

Five wins on the spin have propelled Falkirk up to third place and they will be big favourites to extend that run at home to St Johnstone.

Industry observers note that celtic beaten, Hearts hammered... fans are talking about European qualification, having ended a five-year stint in League 1 in May 2024.

John McGlynn continues to work his magic on a meagre budget, with fresh arrivals Jacob Murrell, Owen Eames, Finley Barbrook and Deniss Melniks hitting the ground running.

Ethan Ross is lapping up a upcoming lease of life, while older heads Scott Bain and Liam Henderson have never been better, although the loss of influential skipper Brad Spencer is a huge blow.

The Perth Saints will be no pushovers. They too are punching above their weight with just four defeats in 13 on their return to the top flight.

Rangers are the only side to beat Simo Valakari's men since a 1-1 draw with Falkirk at McDiarmid Park in mid-September.

That was the first league meeting of the clubs since 2010, but, with such astute managers in place, it looks like this can remain a top-flight rivalry for a good while yet.

Have Hibs turned a corner and have Hearts fallen down a hole?

Marink Reedijk lost his first three games after replacing David Gray, but now the Hibs head coach is looking for a third successive victory at home to Dundee United.

The Easter Road side clambered out of the bottom spot in style, thumping Aberdeen 4-0 at Pittodrie after coming from behind to stun their Edinburgh rivals in the League Cup semi-final.

Hearts went into that game at Hampden as heavy favourites and across the following seven days were outplayed by the team sitting eighth in the Swiss Super League and walloped by Falkirk, ending their 19-month long unbeaten home record in the league.

A growing injury list has hampered Hearts, but Wouter Vrancken's methods are being questioned, with only Kilmarnock conceding more goals in the league.

A visit to Dundee is next and Steven Pressley's much-improved team have only been defeated once at Dens Park so far.

United have also been a breath of fresh air, adopting a fresh swashbuckling style that has yielded four wins and four draws in their past nine games.

Industry observers note that hibs have taken significant strides, particularly in the midfield area, but this will be a real test of their progress. There were 11 goals in the two games against United at Easter Road last season and another major score would not be a surprise.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Foundation Future Industries, a maker of military humanoid robots advised and backed by Eric Trump, failed to pay employees last month as its cash reserves dwindled, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter.

Sources indicate that workers have yet to receive paychecks after San Francisco-based Foundation missed payroll on Oct. 30, said the people, who asked for anonymity to speak candidly about a private tech giant.

The situation has particularly angered some inside the startup because its co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak, borrowed $4.6 million from the company last year to buy a luxury home, money that could have been used to pay workers, the people said.

Public records show that an LLC that names Pathak as sole principal purchased a $4.6 million Sausalito, California, property with "sweeping, cinematic views" of the San Francisco Bay in October 2025.

According to recent reports, A spokesman for Pathak acknowledged receiving a detailed list of the major points from this story on Thursday, but didn't respond to requests for comment. Pathak's previous startup, a fintech firm named Synapse, collapsed in 2024, leaving thousands of Americans locked out of their savings accounts.

Foundation's cash crunch comes at a precarious moment for the firm, which Pathak has said is close to unveiling a next-generation, weapons-ready robot that will help the U.S. compete against Chinese rivals. At the same time, Pathak is seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars in funding at a $3 billion valuation.

Industry observers note that the company has garnered headlines this year for Pathak's claims that his robots could soon take on battlefield tasks in Ukraine or patrol the U.S. border with Mexico. Broadcast interviews and articles about Foundation also include claims that the company has won $24 million in Pentagon contracts.

"What we're about to unveil in the next couple of months [is] going to be the strongest humanoid robot that exists anywhere in the world, including China," Pathak noted in an April television interview.

That April interview introduced Eric Trump, the son of the U.S. president, as a Foundation investor and chief strategy advisor. It is unclear how large his stake is.

Sources indicate that eric Trump and his brother Donald Trump Jr. have invested in an array of defense firms, including makers of military drones and autonomous weapons. A July Washington Post investigation found that startups backed by investment vehicles linked to the brothers had secured at least $3.2 billion in government business.

In a recent development, "We have to win robotics in the United States of America," Eric Trump remarked in April. "When you go up and interact with these robots ... they fist bump you, they high-five you, they follow your commands.".

According to recent reports, eric Trump's involvement in Foundation drew the swift ire of Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who asked whether Foundation won U.S. defense contracts because of nepotism.

"Eric Trump went on FOX to brag about winning ANOTHER multimillion-dollar contract from the Trump administration," Warren stated in an April 23 social media post. "This looks like corruption in plain sight.".

In a recent development, eric Trump didn't respond to requests for comment. His spokesperson recently told the Financial Times that Eric Trump had "no involvement in Foundation's management, operations, strategic decisions or commercial activities, including the solicitation, negotiation, procurement or execution of any government contracts.".

While the Eric Trump announcement created speculation within Foundation that a Democratic-led Congress may look to investigate the tech giant, Foundation itself didn't actually win the $24 million in contracts, despite that assertion being widely reported across news outlets.

Industry observers note that instead, it acquired Florida-based Boardwalk Robotics in late 2024, and government research contracts won by that firm account for the claim, said a person with knowledge of the matter. Foundation used Boardwalk's robot Alex as the basis for its first robot, the Phantom MK-1, this person said.

Foundation's deal for Boardwalk included performance milestones for the robot that haven't been reached, said a separate person with direct knowledge of the deal.

In 2024, CNBC reported that letters Pathak sent to prospective investors cited an imminent investment and $300 million purchase order from General Motors, claims the automaker rejected.

Foundation co-founder Mike LeBlanc said at the time he was "embarrassed" about the marketing materials.

Insiders fret that Foundation could soon fold if Pathak doesn't secure fresh funding. Pathak has been seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars at a $3 billion valuation since at least January.

According to recent reports, pathak is Foundation's sole board member, a structure that has raised concerns among prospective investors about corporate governance, said the people familiar with the matter. He also owns most of the firm's shares.

It has been revealed that that setup allowed Pathak to borrow $4.6 million last year, which he called a short-term loan at the time, the people mentioned. Existing investors are aware of the loan through the organization's financial disclosures, the people said.

In a recent development, "This is what happens in a organization with no governance," mentioned one of the people. "Are you just going to let it ride into the ground, and you ride off into the sunset?".

Foundation also ran out of cash for payroll in August, though employees only had to wait about two days to get paid after the firm secured a bridge loan from an existing investor, the people remarked.

Pathak told employees this week in a memo that he was working on sourcing money to pay back wages.

The manufacturer was founded in April 2024 by Pathak, Tribe Capital CEO Arjun Sethi and LeBlanc, co-founder of Cobalt Robotics, a maker of autonomous security guards, according to a fundraising pitch at the time.

Foundation went on to hire dozens of robotics engineers and artificial intelligence experts, managing to lure some from Tesla and Amazon-owned autonomous vehicle tech giant Zoox.

Before Foundation, Pathak was known as the founder of Synapse, a kind of middleman that enabled fintech firms like Mercury, Dave and YieldStreet to offer savings accounts and credit cards with the help of small community banks.

Synapse was a behind-the-scenes player until its collapse left more than 100,000 Americans with a combined $265 million in deposits locked out of their Federal Deposit Insurance Corp.-backed accounts.

In a recent development, while some customers received partial payments during Synapse's bankruptcy proceedings, thousands remain without access to their money after more than two years. A bankruptcy trustee, the former FDIC Chair Jelena McWilliams, mentioned as much as $96 million in customer funds went missing.

Industry observers note that the bankruptcy proceedings concluded last year without uncovering where the funds went; Pathak blamed a banking partner named Evolve, and Evolve blamed Synapse for the mess. U.S. regulators didn't intervene until the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau sued Synapse last year, opening up a $55 million fund for customer relief.

Pathak withdrew $320,000 in loans from Synapse as it spiraled toward bankruptcy in 2024 amid disputes over unmatched ledgers, according to the consultant and independent journalist Jason Mikula.

Industry observers note that federal prosecutors convened a grand jury to investigate possible criminal misconduct at Synapse, The Wall Street Journal reported last year. The Journal report didn't mention Pathak specifically.

The controversy didn't dissuade Eric Trump from investing in Foundation and Pathak, who he called a friend in the April broadcast interview.

Recent findings suggest that "I walked into his factory, and I couldn't believe what I saw," Eric Trump mentioned. "I'm telling you, he's doing a phenomenal job.".

  • One afternoon in the fall of 2023—fifteen days after Hamas’ brutal October 7 attacks—the founder of the right-wing news aggregator Visegrad24, Stefan Tompson, texted a confidant to work out some private thoughts on what he called “the Israel situation.” Over the previous two weeks of carnage in the Middle East, Tompson’s team had pulled off a social media coup, and now he seemed to be wrestling with how to wield his channel’s newfound influence.
  • Almost from the moment Hamas paragliders first touched down in Israel, Visegrad24—then a three-year old Polish account ostensibly dedicated to “curating news, politics, current affairs, history, and culture from Central and Eastern Europe”—had managed to swoop in and dominate X’s breaking-news discussion of the war in Gaza.
  • Industry observers note that in the conflict’s first three days, V24’s team worked around the clock to pump out nearly 400 posts on the violence: a mix of terse news updates, soft tributes to Israeli victims, and—above all—rage-bait videos showing allegedly “pro-Hamas” demonstrations in cities across the West.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One afternoon in the fall of 2023—fifteen days after Hamas’ brutal October 7 attacks—the founder of the right-wing news aggregator Visegrad24, Stefan Tompson, texted a confidant to work out some private thoughts on what he called “the Israel situation.” Over the previous two weeks of carnage in the Middle East, Tompson’s team had pulled off a social media coup, and now he seemed to be wrestling with how to wield his channel’s newfound influence.

Almost from the moment Hamas paragliders first touched down in Israel, Visegrad24—then a three-year old Polish account ostensibly dedicated to “curating news, politics, current affairs, history, and culture from Central and Eastern Europe”—had managed to swoop in and dominate X’s breaking-news discussion of the war in Gaza.

Industry observers note that in the conflict’s first three days, V24’s team worked around the clock to pump out nearly 400 posts on the violence: a mix of terse news updates, soft tributes to Israeli victims, and—above all—rage-bait videos showing allegedly “pro-Hamas” demonstrations in cities across the West. According to a rapid analysis that month by media researchers at the University of Washington, those 400 posts racked up an astonishing 370 million views. As the UW researchers framed it, a 641,000-follower Polish account had just catapulted itself atop a list of “fresh elites” on X, momentarily trouncing the reach of legacy outlets with follower counts in the tens of millions, like CNN, The New York Times, and the BBC.

It has been revealed that more to the point, Visegrad had also established itself overnight as one of the most influential pro-Israel accounts on X. And that’s what seemed to be giving Tompson pause.

“With the Israel situation,” Tompson texted his colleague, “I do loathe Hamas, and it’s been the perfect excuse to show the scale of Muslim infiltration in the west” (a long-standing editorial priority for Tompson and his team). But Tompson seemed wary that Israel was already angling for a wider regional conflict. “Personally I want that war to be contained where it is,” Tompson wrote. “And the Israelis do seem to be doing some vicious things.”.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, the founder reasoned a way through his qualms. In another message from the same day, the cigar-smoking, cravat-wearing, thirtysomething Tompson wrote to the same confidant—whom I’ll call Boris—to spell out how he’d landed with regard to V24’s “editorial line” on Israel. As Tompson saw it, V24 had been faced with “four options” once the war started:.

In a recent development, 1. Say nothing;2. Be objective—get hated by both sides;3. Pro Muslim—there are 1.5 billion of them;4. Pro Israel—There are fewer but also they have a lot of influence and money.

In choosing between those options, Tompson laid out a blunt motivation: “My goal is to fundraise off of this,” he wrote.

It has been revealed that covering Gaza did fit nicely with V24’s long-standing brand of anti-Muslim, anti-migrant, Western-chauvinist content. (“The beauty of this war is that it allows us to criticize slims—especially those in Europe—without any consequences,” Tompson would later write, using a shorthand slur for Muslims.) But now he seemed to have his eyes on a bigger opportunity: using Visegrad’s “new elite” status to rake in money from some of Israel’s most powerful supporters in Silicon Valley and beyond.

And according to an extensive trove of V24 financial records, internal communications, screenshots from group chats, and correspondence with donors, all reviewed by WIRED, Tompson promptly succeeded at exactly that.

Over the past six years, Visegrad24 has become a strangely ubiquitous force in right-wing social media, its feed a reliable kaleidoscope of dehumanized, brown-skinned aggressors and their alleged depredations against innocent, often white-skinned victims, alongside global news from a nationalist perspective. On any given day, V24 might show you a stomach-turning video of a camel being abused at a wedding in the West Bank, a parade of cell phone clips showing violent crimes being committed by alleged “migrants” all across Europe, or an interview about the Great Replacement Theory.

Sources indicate that from its headquarters in Warsaw, V24’s lean pseudo-news operation has proven itself almost preternaturally adept at virality on Elon Musk’s X. It even seems to have become one of the oligarch’s own favorite accounts. For a period after November 2024, Musk became especially fixated on British far-right politics, posting nonstop about “rape gangs” of South Asian men allegedly grooming British girls. To better understand Musk’s influences at the time, WIRED partnered with the research firm Bright Data to analyze his interactions with some 30 prominent European far-right accounts over a 45-day period ending in January 2025; we found that Musk engaged with Visegrad24, a major font of “grooming gangs” content, at least three times more than any other account on the list. Another dubious mark of distinction for V24: Of all the billion-plus accounts on X, Visegrad ranks 32nd in the number of community notes—crowdsourced fact checks—that have been attached to its posts.

Sources indicate that but in tandem with its drumbeat of demonized migrants, V24 has also excelled at capitalizing on the information wars that inevitably form around real, bloody conflicts like those in Ukraine, Gaza, and now Iran. The documents obtained by WIRED—to which Tompson responded with a blanket denial and an email from a lawyer—shed an intimate light on how this playbook evolved over the course of V24’s rapid rise. They provide an unvarnished case study of life inside today’s fractured and erratic right-wing mediasphere. And they reveal how the right kind of online influence, even when it’s strategically acquired by an entity just barely above the gutter of white nationalism, can command support from some of the most powerful people in the world.

In late November 2023, Tompson wrote to Boris with some exciting news. “Jewish VCs have created a group,” he texted. “Several. I’m in two of those groups that actively push back against founders who have supported Palestine.” In another message he described one of these encrypted text threads as “85 people. 84 Jews and me.”.

It has been revealed that “They are slowly reaching out directly … Usually they want a retweet,” he wrote to Boris. “V24 is such a major part of the Israeli PR they all know what it is now.”.

“You’re in the belly of the beast now,” replied Boris (who requested anonymity for fear of legal retaliation).

One of the groups to which Tompson gained entry was called Jewish Alliances, described by one of its members—someone going by the handle Sean Rad, which is the name of a Tinder cofounder—as a space to “bring together Jews and non-Jews working together to fight antisemitism.”.

It has been revealed that on Jewish Alliances, Tompson came personally recommended by Shaun Maguire, a general partner at Sequoia Capital who led the firm’s investments in Elon Musk–affiliated companies. Like V24, Maguire had become vociferously pro-Israel after October 7—later explaining that the attacks galvanized him to engage in “information warfare” for the country. Maguire had even made introductions that eventually helped connect the Israel Defense Forces with Musk’s Starlink satellite communication network in the earliest days of the Gaza war. And now, on Jewish Alliances, he was throwing some weight behind V24.

In a recent development, “Stefan / Visegrad is an incredible account if you’re not already following,” Maguire told the group thread. Privately, Maguire told Tompson, “I’ll give u $25k and try to raise the rest.” (Maguire later told WIRED that he ultimately had to stop short of making his donation. “I would have loved to donate to Visegrad, as I think their content is excellent, but I wasn't able to for compliance reasons.”).

As for the other elite group chat that Tompson claims he was invited to join, it appears to have been even more rarefied. In December that year, Tompson sent Boris a screenshot of a blurb from a Puck newsletter, headlined “The In-Crowd’s Hottest Text Thread.” Tompson had circled the item in red with an arrow pointing at it.

“I learned this week that hundreds of the most powerful figures from Silicon Valley, Wall Street, and Hollywood have joined a sprawling, informal WhatsApp thread to share thoughts on how to build support for Israel and combat antisemitism following the attacks of October 7,” wrote media reporter Dylan Byers in the blurb. “The group, which is called Builders for Israel, includes the likes of Sheryl Sandberg, Bill Ackman, and David Marcus.”.

“And Stefan Tompson 😂,” Boris replied, to which Tompson responded with his own laughing emoji.

On the two group chats, Tompson sometimes gawked at the proceedings, sending Boris screenshots of what he was witnessing. On November 24, one member posted the following message to the group: “I bought some domains. If anyone would like them to redirect to appropriate content lmk.”.

The member then listed out a series of five urls: “longlivetheintifada.com, wechargeyouwithgenocide.com, palestineisourhome.com, fromtherivertothesee.com, fromtheriver2theseapalestinewillbefree.com.”.

“Btw this is available albeit $75k,” the member went on, before posting a screenshot showing a listing for the domain name “Allahuakbar.com.”.

Tompson himself responded inside the group. “Oh this has so much potential! 💀” he wrote.

It has been revealed that (A review of public web domain records indicates that all five of the first urls listed here were registered through GoDaddy using Domains by Proxy, a service that allows domain registrants to hide their personal contact information. The records show that all five were created on November 22, 2023, in two batches 33 minutes apart. It’s unclear whether anyone bought Allahuakbar.com, whose owner is also hidden behind the proxy service, but its registration record was last updated on November 28, 2023.).

Recent findings suggest that as a platform for fundraising, the two group chats appear to have paid off pretty handsomely for Visegrad24. “Should have 75k on Monday,” Tompson wrote to Boris on November 18. There was $50,000 coming from “a very private man” at the Silicon Valley fintech investment firm Ribbit Capital. Ribbit's founder is Meyer “Micky” Malka, an early investor in Coinbase and promoter of crypto. Tompson would later tell Boris that Malka was allegedly planning to donate an additional $200,000. Financial records show donations of $50,000 and $200,000 roughly lining up with Tompson's messages, but Malka did not respond to requests for comment. Records indicate that Tompson also secured a $20,000 donation from the investment firm Hindenberg Research, with an additional $15,000 linked to an email address associated with the firm’s founder, the prominent Wall Street short seller Nathan Anderson. Tompson also claimed he had a “soft commitment” from the Israeli American investor Daniel Gross, a former AI lead at both Apple and Y Combinator. (Anderson did not respond to requests for comment; Gross’s representatives remarked they have no record of a donation.).

Notifications from GiveButter, a site Tompson used for soliciting contributions, show that other donations were linked to email addresses associated with SimpleVenue CEO Michael Sinensky, Warby Parker founder Neil Blumenthal, Wix president Nir Zohar, Lux Capital cofounder Josh Wolfe, and deep tech venture capitalist Matt Ocko.

(Sinensky and Blumenthal declined to comment, and Zohar’s representatives said they had no record of him donating. Wolfe and Ocko neither confirmed nor denied that they’d given money to V24, but both came back with remarkably similar responses, primarily taking issue with WIRED’s characterization of whether Visegrad is “far right.” “I don't fund or support ‘far right’ groups,” Wolfe wrote, “and thankfully Stefan and Visegard24 are pro-democracy, pro-Western values, pro-peace and prosperity.” Wrote Ocko: “Even cursory research indicates that neither Mr. Tompson, nor Visegrad24 are affiliated with or support anything other than: classical liberal Western values, including the rule of law; the defense of democratic polities from terror and autocracies … peace and prosperity for all law-abiding and civilized people; opposition to horrific antisemitism and terrorist exaltation.”).

It has been revealed that while Tompson was fundraising away with his group-chat contacts, Boris wrote with a question. “By the way, should I take Middle Eastern money?” he asked, mentioning opportunities to raise funds from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

“100 percent yes. Play both sides,” Tompson mentioned. “I do the Jewish side. You do Arabs.”.

To receive its donations, V24 set up an organization under the 501(c)(3) umbrella called the Intermarium Foundation, headquartered in Pennsylvania but domiciled in Delaware. Over the next year and more, over a million dollars poured in. Much of the money, including some of the largest sums, appears to have come in through “donor advised funds”—“dark money” philanthropic vehicles that allow donors to hide their identities, even from the recipients of their cash. Foundation documents show that in November 2024, the organization received $175,000 from DonorsTrust, a fund closely aligned with the Trump administration’s priorities, often referred to as the “dark money ATM” of the American right. Documents also suggest that V24 received $172,000 from the Giving Back Fund, which describes itself as a “national nonprofit organization that encourages and facilitates charitable giving by professional athletes, celebrities, high-net-worth individuals, existing nonprofit organizations, corporations, and others.”.

A London-born self-described “Polish South African” who was “educated in French schools,” Tompson founded Visegrad24 in early 2020. He'd moved to Warsaw from London in the mid-2010s, having worked as a PR strategist on the “Leave” side of the Brexit campaign, according to Gizmodo. Tompson’s great-grandfather, he has stated, was the Polish ambassador to England at the time of the Nazi invasion. Between the war and the communist takeover of Poland, the family was left stranded abroad for three generations. In a 2024 interview with Jewish Insider, Tompson referred to his arrival in Warsaw as his “own version of aliyah,” the Hebrew word used to describe a Jewish person’s immigration to Israel.

It has been revealed that tompson’s homecoming took place just as Poland was attempting to aggressively pattern itself after Viktor Orban’s Hungary. In 2015, the illiberal, nationalist Law and Justice Party swept Polish elections and set about packing courts, hollowing institutions, and seizing control of Polish state radio, newspapers, and television—turning the latter into nakedly xenophobic, anti-opposition, and often antisemitic propaganda organs.

According to recent reports, with his taste for cravats and posh Barbour jackets, Tompson found an audience on Polish state TV documentaries extolling the country’s grand cultural heritage. He started a PR agency called Bracia Tompson SC, and according to the investigative site VSquare, he made short films with the support of something called the Institute for the Legacy of Polish National Thought, described by the Polish news outlet Polytka as a slush fund for the governing party.

Tompson also spent the late 2010s working on what he described as a “three-hour documentary” about his father’s ancestral home, South Africa—a country whose quality of life, Tompson claimed in a 2019 Polish radio interview, is worse today than under apartheid. The documentary project was reportedly titled African Volhynia, after an area in Central Europe where Poles suffered historic massacres, land dispossession, and ethnic cleansing—a framing that, to some observers, strongly suggests that Tompson was packaging a South African “white genocide” narrative for a Polish audience. The full documentary, however, was never released.

Instead, Tompson shifted focus to launch Visegrad24 in January 2020, with a logo closely mirroring the South African outlet News24. The name Visegrad is a reference to the Visegrad Group, an informal diplomatic bloc of four Central European nations that includes Poland and Hungary. In 2020, it was Poland’s turn to occupy the rotating presidency of the alliance—and V24 appears to have served a promotional function. When V24’s Facebook page was briefly blocked for violating community standards in 2021, the Polish deputy minister of foreign affairs spoke up for the account. “The Visegrad24 profile is not an official profile of the Visegrad Group or the Polish presidency of the Visegrad Group,” he told a Polish radio station. “However, we appreciate it for its promotion of the group’s activities.”.

One of Tompson’s main partners in the enterprise was a Polish journalist named Adam Starzynski, the former proprietor of an ultra-right-wing Twitter account called @BasedPoland and reportedly a fellow board member at something called the State of Poland Foundation. Their third, more silent founder was Tompson’s brother Jan. Tompson’s sister Alexandra also became involved, sometimes serving as a de facto legal rep.

In its early years, Visegrad24 posted roughly in line with the Law and Justice Party’s priorities—positively about Poland’s abortion ban, negatively about migrants, fulsomely about Christianity and Hungarian fertility rates—and was tagged frequently by party officials, according to Polish investigative site OKO.Press.

According to recent reports, but Tompson harbored bigger ambitions, as well as some apparent personal struggles. In early 2022, Visegrad’s core team escaped the Polish winter by renting a house together in the Canary Islands—during which time Tompson was said to be “undergoing acute drug withdrawal and was in a very vulnerable state,” according to an email later written by Alexandra and reviewed by WIRED. (In a couple of messages, Tompson refers to a time in his life when he was “on coke.”).

It has been revealed that the team had been in Gran Canaria for about a month when something momentous happened: Vladimir Putin invaded Ukraine. In the early morning hours of February 24, they woke up to images of Russian tanks crossing Ukraine’s borders. They immediately began pushing out an intense volume of news and clickbait.

Bit by bit, Visegrad started gaining international traction—and international notoriety for spreading fake news. On February 25, Visegrad tweeted “PornHub cockblocks Russian consumers,” alleging that Russian porn seekers “were presented with a message saying the content is blocked along with a Ukrainian flag and a message of support to Ukraine”—a rumor that was debunked by Snopes and other online fact-checkers. Then, about a week later, V24 tweeted that actor Leonardo DiCaprio had donated $10 million to Ukraine in honor of his grandmother from Odesa. (DiCaprio made no such donation, and there is no evidence of such a grandmother.) Articles debunking V24’s claim promptly appeared on Snopes and CNN.

This first brush with global virality came with risks. Elon Musk didn’t own Twitter yet, and content moderation was strict. “I’m really stressing out over v24,” Tompson wrote in an internal WhatsApp group named Gran Canaria. But rather than get shut down, V24 lived to see its follower count triple, growing from 80,000 to 250,000 in weeks.

V24’s boosted reach didn’t bring an end to Tompson’s frustrations, however. He appeared dissatisfied with the liberal followers that came along with being such a prominent pro-Ukrainian account. And he also seemed to be running into patronage problems: In 2022, the Polish news outlet Wiadomości revealed that the office of Polish prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki had tried to allocate about $300,000 for “the implementation of the public project titled ‘Visegrad24,’” sending money to a sports and fitness NGO called the Action-Life Foundation. Then, in 2023, according to OKO.press, Morawiecki’s office appears to have sent a bit under $600,000 for a “media center” at the Action-Life Foundation—which appeared, yet again, to be a carve-out for a V24-affiliated project. This time the grant was recalled after public outcry. (In an interview, Tompson has mentioned he “never had a penny to run Visegrad” from the Polish state.) In October 2023, the Law & Justice Party lost its majority in parliament, ending eight years of right-wing dominance over Polish government purse strings.

Sources indicate that by that fall, Tompson seems to have realized that V24’s Canary Islands posting blitz had yielded a huge bump in influence that they’d failed to monetize. In terms of fundraising, Tompson told Boris, “we missed the boat with Ukraine.” So when V24 repeated its flood-the-zone strategy with the October 7 attacks, Tompson seemed determined not to skip the next step.

By early 2024, Tompson was sitting down in Tel Aviv for a podcast interview with the American-born Israeli venture capitalist Michael Eisenberg—often billed as an informal adviser to Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Less than six months had passed since October 7, and Tompson was on his way to becoming a minor celebrity among friends of Israel. “Meet the Man Who Shapes Millions of Twitter Customers’ view of Israel’s war,” ran the headline of a story in the Jewish Chronicle, which went on to describe a series of V24 videos Tompson’s team had been filming on the streets of the West Bank. “Anyone who notes it is an apartheid state in Israel and the Palestinian people are subjugated should go to Ramallah,” Tompson told the news outlet. “There were Maseratis and Mercedes and a brand-fresh shopping mall.” As of that month, at least 28,473 Palestinians had been killed in Gaza since October 7, and at least 388 had been killed in the West Bank, Israel, and East Jerusalem, according to the United Nations.

Recent findings suggest that tompson was also busily fundraising. “The west is under attack,” claimed a sleek V24 donor pitch deck dated August 2024 and later reviewed by WIRED. “We face two major adversaries: radical progressives” and “nefarious States (Russia, Iran, China, Qatar).” The pitch deck called V24 “the frontier of modern journalism for western values.”.

Industry observers note that one pitch deck promoted “Project Q,” a social media campaign against Qatar. In a single month, Project Q had delivered “97 posts about Qatar across multiple accounts,” 12 original pieces of video content, including a “viral” short featuring the British anti-Islamic activist Tommy Robinson, video essays, and an instance of then Polish MEP Michał Dworczyk condemning Qatar in a speech.

V24 also boasted that it was building “a network of Muslim and Arab influencers to push content,” including pro-Israel voices Loay Alshareef, Nuseir Yassin, Luai Ahmed, and YouTuber “Apostate Prophet,” the latter an ex-Muslim interviewee on V24’s YouTube.

Then there was the Project Veritas–style hidden-camera news operation Tompson had introduced, called V24 Investigations, run by the ex-Project Veritas board member Matthew Tyrmand. In the spring of 2024, V24 Investigations fanned out across American university campuses amid pro-Palestine protests to make unflattering, Project Veritas–style videos of student activists, part of a larger V24 effort to expand its YouTube presence.

But in 2025 and 2026, Visegrad would see more opportunity to draw on a traditional area of strength—breaking war news on X.

On June 13, 2025, Israel leaped into the wider conflict that Tompson had initially been afraid of: That morning, Tel Aviv brutally ambushed Iran with an onslaught of synchronized assassinations, air raids, and drone strikes—and V24 aggressively posted through it on X. But this time, alongside its fairly typical mix of war porn and mockery of pro-Palestinian protesters, a somewhat unusual motif ran through Visegrad’s social coverage of the war: Enthusiasm for restoring the leadership of Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran’s last Shah.

Sources indicate that V24 even played a bit part in the social media war to influence US president Donald Trump as he toyed with joining Israel’s fight. On the fifth day of the war—after Trump had stated on Truth Social, “We know exactly where the so-called ‘Supreme Leader’ is hiding”—Visegrad chimed in with a post on X seemingly tailor-made to sweeten the option of regime change:.

In a recent development, incoming reports of Iranian military officers seeking contact with Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi to declare their intent to defect. They also want to pledge their allegiance to His Majesty and his mission to lead the transition to democracy in Iran after the regime’s fall.

Visegrad’s post received more than a million views and was shared nearly 3,000 times.

When Trump finally did make his move four days later, dropping a set of “bunker buster” bombs on Iranian nuclear sites, V24 posted an image of the Islamic Republic’s flag being torn away to reveal that of the Pahlavi monarchy and the words “It’s time” (2.4 million views, 3,600 shares).

Sources indicate that why the outsize focus on the sexagenarian exiled son of a former dictator? Pahlavi does enjoy a certain amount of organic political support among the Iranian diaspora. But he’s also been held up at times as Israel’s preferred leader for Iran. In October 2025, Haaretz, TheMarker, and the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab reported that Israel’s government was likely behind a massive Persian-language “influence operation” to simulate online support for Pahlavi using bots, synchronized posting campaigns, and artificial intelligence—all “as part of an even broader Israeli campaign to influence the social media discourse.”.

V24’s own pro-Pahlavi posting binge was underway at the same time. When asked whether V24 had received any funding from Pahlavi’s network, Tompson responded by saying, “I wasn’t aware that Reza Pahlavi was a foreign state.” When asked whether he had received any money from Israel directly, Tompson replied with an apparent joke. “Yes,” he wrote, “Benjamin Netanyahu personally hands me money for every post on Visegrad24.”.

In the three years since October 7, Visegrad24’s follower count has swelled to 2.1 million on X. But even as Musk’s platform has stubbornly remained V24’s only real area of strength, it has also become a more contested one since 2023. “They’re operating in an extremely competitive space,” claims Ryan Broderick, the founder of the Garbage Day newsletter, which tracks the online media ecosystem.

In recent years, with the rise of open-source-intelligence “monitoring the situation” accounts on X—essentially breaking-news channels run by hyper-online finance people—real-time coverage of crises and conflicts has become more of a crowded market, says Broderick. Today, he figures, an October 7–style V24 posting blitz would have a harder time breaking through. At the same time, V24’s other stock and trade—xenophobic posts about migrants—is easily upstaged by countless accounts that are more nakedly, brazenly racist.

Meanwhile, support for Israel has only become a more isolating position to occupy on the global far right, which has leaned further and further into its natural affinity for noxious antisemitism. (In 2025, Tompson appears to have met up in Turkey with another right-wing video creator named Lord Miles—a British self-styled adventurer who denigrates many of the same ethnic groups that V24 does, only with the addition of being blatantly antisemitic. According to Lord Miles, the two were set to collaborate on a video. But then Tompson started talking about raising six-figure sums from a pro-Israel “WhatsApp group chat,” and Lord Miles bolted from the scene, later posting about the episode on X.).

Industry observers note that relatively early in its reporting on V24, WIRED reached out to some people who know Tompson, including an ex-partner. Shortly afterward, Tompson called back from her phone. “That’s not how we do things in South Africa, my friend,” he said. “I don’t like it. I find it creepy; I find it weird.” He then offered to pay for a flight to Warsaw for an on-the-record interview with him—an offer WIRED declined, given journalistic standards against accepting money from sources. “Are you not a man, my friend?” Tompson said. “I’m very upset you have disrespected me.”.

When WIRED later got in touch to arrange a concrete date for a phone interview, Tompson asked if he could be sent questions in advance. When WIRED refused, citing standard editorial practice, Tompson balked. “Not really interested in you wasting my time old sport,” he wrote, “What exactly is the incentive for me to give you any more of my time, generosity or politeness?” He signed off the message with the words, “praying that you find Christ, who redeems all, including the likes of sinning wretches like myself.”.

It has been revealed that he later turned WIRED’s reporter’s request for an interview around. “Now I am kindly offering you the opportunity to answer some questions,” he wrote. “It’s a generous offer, which will allow you to give your perspective on things and answer some notable questions about your behavior, your lifestyle, your funding, and some other details that are an important reflection of you who are as a person.” WIRED declined.

NASA's Voyager 1 released second, so how did it beat Voyager 2 to a light-day by nearly a decade?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (907 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035.
  • 18, Voyager 1 will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full light-day (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers).
  • But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035. Why the big difference?

Sources indicate that on Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full light-day (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal — so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky.

But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer? It comes down to choices made for speed and science during the twin missions' nearly 50-year journey, specifically during the first bit when they were flying by planets. The result is Voyager 1 is zooming out at a speed of 3.5 Earth-sun distances (astronomical units a year), while Voyager 2 has a more stately speed of 3.1 Earth-sun distances, according to NASA.

The original aim of both the spacecraft, which debuted about two weeks apart in 1977 with Voyager 2 going first, was to look at Jupiter and Saturn. If funding persisted, which it did, the hope was to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune, taking advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Voyager 1, by contrast, made a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings and the prebiotic (pre-life-chemistry) moon of Titan, before flying outside the plane of the solar system.

It has been revealed that NASA had a range of trajectory options to consider when launching the spacecraft, and elected to bring Voyager 1 at a faster trajectory — as illustrated in this video by Britannica, where you can quickly see the spacecraft overtaking Voyager 2 on its way to Jupiter even though Voyager 1. Voyager 1 arrived at Jupiter on March 5, 1979 while Voyager 2 got there four months later on July 9.

Each of the spacecraft then performed a "gravity assist"—a sort of slingshot around the planet in which they took a tiny bit of momentum from Jupiter to gain speed as the spacecraft flew to Saturn. This technique is used constantly, such as recently when the ESCAPADE Mars mission flew two spacecraft by Earth on the way to the Red Planet, as it allows spacecraft to gain speed while saving on fuel. The planets themselves don't slow down that much.

"Because the planet is so much more massive than the spacecraft, the transfer doesn't affect the planet to any measurable extent, but to the spacecraft it's a big deal," the Planetary Society wrote. "For example, we can calculate that during the Voyager encounters with Jupiter in 1979, Jupiter slowed down by roughly 10 to the -24th power kilometers per second — a change much too small to measure.".

"But each Voyager gained about 10 km/s [6.2 miles/s], a pretty major number," the society continued about the Jupiter encounter. This was "enough to put them on a fast path to Saturn — and in the case of Voyager 2, to Uranus and Neptune as well — and eventual escape from the solar system.".

With each flyby, the two spacecraft picked up speed with a single exception — during Voyager 2's encounter of Neptune. That's because the spacecraft made a turn to fly by Triton. The maneuver brought Voyager 2 over Neptune's north pole, before it turned and then was directed to begin "plunging down, out of the plane of the solar system," losing speed along the way.

Voyager 2, in fact, did not have enough speed to leave the solar system until it flew by Jupiter. "It gained about 10 km/s at Jupiter, about 5 km/s at Saturn, about 2 km/s at Uranus, and lost about 2 km/s at Neptune," the Planetary Society wrote of the speeds, which are 6.21 miles/s, 3.11 miles/s, 1.24 miles/s and a loss of 1.24 miles/s, respectively.

According to recent reports, at any rate, these fast speeds allowed both spacecraft not only to go fast, but to eventually reach interstellar space in 2012 (Voyager 1) and 2018 (Voyager 2), respectively. With the light-day milestone now reached by Voyager 1, it is anticipated the spacecraft could work into the 2030s, as long as their nuclear power sources can last.

NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which manages the mission, has been carefully turning off instruments as required, and recently did a "Major Bang" procedure on both spacecraft to redistribute power supplies as best as possible. The idea is to maximize science return on both spacecraft, the only interstellar messengers we have, for as long as possible.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight debuts on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tony Mowbray started his managerial career with Hibernian.

The overwhelming support from the world of football for Blackburn Rovers boss Tony Mowbray has come as no surprise to interim head coach Damien Johnson.

Mowbray announced on Wednesday he was stepping back from his role at the Championship club because of health concerns with Johnson and Mike Dodds taking charge "for the time being".

The news sparked an outpouring of messages of support from EFL clubs and further afield.

"To someone like me, it's not a surprise," Johnson noted.

"I've known him for over 10 years, but I think people who have only known him in this club for the four or five months he's been in, they can see that. That's just the impact Tony has on people, it's just a testament to Tony and his nature and how he is and how he treats people.".

Mowbray, 62, returned to Ewood Park in June for a second spell as head coach and has taken them to 13th place in the Championship after they finished just five points clear of the relegation zone last season.

The former Middlesbrough and West Brom boss had previously taken time out of the game during his spell as Birmingham City boss in early 2024 following a health scare, and later revealed he had been undergoing treatment for bowel cancer.

Boro head coach Kim Hellberg was one of the first to send his best wishes to one of his predecessors.

"He's a brilliant guy. It was really good to meet him and he was absolutely brilliant every time I've talked to him," Hellberg said.

"He's a brilliant football coach. He's done a lot of good things. He's a brilliant human being and you can see everyone knows that.".

Rovers have won five of their past nine league games with Johnson crediting Mowbray's impact at the club for creating a more positive atmosphere.

"When the statement came out there was concern - we care a lot about Tony and it was a little bit of a shock - we want what's best for him at this time," Johnson told BBC Radio Lancashire.

"Tony has built a real bond with the whole group and with everyone at the whole club, so there was naturally concern for him and a bit of emotion for a day or so but we all hold him in the highest regard - we hope he's given the privacy he needs.

In a recent development, "He sent a private message to the players which was read out today [Friday] and they appreciated it. He's sent some private messages to staff but Tony's allowed us just to get on, he'll be allowed the time he needs and we'll just get on with the game.".

Blackburn visit Burnley on Sunday (12:00 GMT) hoping to end a 10-game winless run against their Lancashire rivals, who have not won a home game in the league since 18 October last year.

Johnson says the match is their main focus rather than what may happen with the managerial situation down the line.

Industry observers note that "We've just been focused fully on the game, we know it's a huge game and we've been working with the team throughout the week. The discussions have been about the game and nothing else," he added.

Meanwhile, Blackburn are set to be without goalkeeper Balazs Toth until the new year after he told Hungarian media, external he suffered a hand injury while playing for his national side against Northern Ireland on Tuesday.

"The situation is not that good, but for now it looks like I will be able to avoid surgery," he stated before travelling back to England to have the injury assessed by Blackburn.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google and Apple might be competitors, but they can play nice sometimes.
  • For example, Google just announced that you can now use Gemini AI to control a Mac computer.
  • How can customers take advantage of Gemini computer use for MacBooks, Mac Mini, and iMac devices?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google and Apple might be competitors, but they can play nice sometimes.

For example, Google just announced that you can now use Gemini AI to control a Mac computer. With this new feature, you can give Gemini commands and it will root through your files, access your apps, and browse the web to complete whatever tasks you've asked it to perform. All of this is facilitated by the Gemini app for macOS 27 Golden Gate, per Google's press release.

How can customers take advantage of Gemini computer use for MacBooks, Mac Mini, and iMac devices?

Google provided several examples in an announcement blog post, such as asking Gemini to take a child's sketch of a butterfly and render it polygonally using the 3D modeling program Blender. Once the request is processed, Gemini performs the task in an isolated background window with a preview display right in the Gemini app, allowing you to watch it perform the task in real-time. However, as Google noted, you also retain full use of your Mac while this is happening, allowing owners to continue browsing, typing, and completing other types of work.

In a recent development, while this may be a boon to Gemini power owners who own devices like the upcoming MacBook Pro OLED, it's worth noting that giving an AI agent full access to all your local files and apps carries inherent risks. Google gives users the ability to freely choose which apps Gemini has access to, alongside the ability to watch the process as it unfolds, in case something goes wrong. So, you can pause Gemini if it's doing something you don't like, and approve decisions before they're made. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile Products available for purchase through affiliate links. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

It should also be noted that Google is playing catch-up with this announcement. Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic already offer this type of agentic feature, so Google's just a tad late to the party.

Google also just upgraded Gemini with even more task-completing power this week, introducing Gemini Tasks, a feature in the AI chatbot that lets it complete tasks for browser owners (a feature not to be confused with Google Tasks).

Recent findings suggest that per Google, the new computer use feature is rolling out immediately for English customers in the Gemini app, though it requires a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription. Users will need a Mac device with Apple Silicon and macOS Sequoia 15.0 or later.

To get started, visit gemini.google/mac.

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was just six months ago that Graham Potter was deemed the man to usher in a fresh, exciting era at Chelsea.
  • The club’s new ownership group, led by American businessman Todd Boehly, had enticed Potter away from Brighton with the promise of managing one of the most lucrative teams in world soccer.
  • More than $600 million was spent on bringing significant-name players to the club and Potter, one of the most exciting young managers in the Premier League, was to mold them into a winning machine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was just six months ago that Graham Potter was deemed the man to usher in a fresh, exciting era at Chelsea.

The club’s new ownership group, led by American businessman Todd Boehly, had enticed Potter away from Brighton with the promise of managing one of the most lucrative teams in world soccer.

More than $600 million was spent on bringing significant-name players to the club and Potter, one of the most exciting young managers in the Premier League, was to mold them into a winning machine.

Chelsea has spent over $600 million on new signings. Here's why that's significant.

But, on Sunday, the club revealed that it had sacked its manager after an underwhelming spell in charge.

Potter managed to win just 10 of the 28 league matches this season and leaves the team 11th in the Premier League table.

In recent weeks, players had looked a shadow of their former selves and many fans had lost confidence that Potter’s initiative for the club could ever work.

Eventually, after previously sticking by its manager, Blues ownership agreed.

“On behalf of everyone at the club, we want to thank Graham sincerely for his contribution to Chelsea,” the club’s co-owners Todd Boehly and Behdad Eghbali remarked in a statement.

“We have the highest degree of respect for Graham as a coach and as a person. He has always conducted himself with professionalism and integrity and we are all disappointed in this outcome.”.

In his previous role as Brighton manager, Potter was given time to stamp his identity on the squad.

The club was punching above its weight financially and, as a result, carefully selected newly introduced signings which would compliment Potter’s style of play.

The approach paid off as the team became an established Premier League outfit which has gone on to greater things this season – the Seagulls currently sit sixth in the league and in the UEFA Conference League qualification spot.

At Chelsea, it seemed the complete opposite.

As was the case under previous owner Roman Abramovich, the club expected instant results and used its financial weight to sign a number of high-profile names, including the likes of Enzo Fernández and Mykhailo Mudryk.

Despite his impressive CV, Potter had never managed superstars and suddenly found himself in a changing room with multiple.

The scatter gun approach to recruitment also left the team lacking balance and organization with Potter failing to get a tune out of a team busting with talent.

In truth, many had raised an eyebrow when Potter, inexperienced at the very top level, was chosen to replace Thomas Tuchel as manager.

Despite falling out of favor with fans by the end of his tenure, Tuchel had guided Chelsea to the Champions League title in 2021 and is still considered by many as one of the best coaches in the world.

The German has gone on to sign with Bavarian giant Bayern Munich through the 2024/25 season and recently told reporters he needed “quite a bit of time to distance himself from Chelsea” because leaving the club had hurt him.

Bayern Munich sacks manager Julian Nagelsmann, appoints Thomas Tuchel.

“Todd [Boehly] mentioned he would be different to Roman [Abramovich],” former Liverpool player and current pundit Jamie Carragher wrote on Twitter.

Industry observers note that “I feel for Graham Potter, but it was inevitable. You don’t change Tuchel for Potter. Ridiculous decision to start with.”.

With 10 games left in the league and a Champions League quarterfinal against Real Madrid on the horizon, Chelsea still has plenty to play for.

Assistant coach Bruno Saltor will take over on an interim basis, but Boehly and his team must now look for a long-term replacement capable – and willing – to bring order to Chelsea’s chaos.

Potter’s sacking is yet another sign of just how transient managers can be in the top-flight of English football, especially when results aren’t instantaneous.

There has now been a record 12 sackings in the Premier League so far this season, with Potter leaving his position the same day Leicester boss Brendan Rodgers was sacked from his.

The previous record was 10 manager changes in a single season, set in four other campaigns, most recently in 2017/18.

Their individual totals will be shown on the guest leaderboard below - with FM 27 going top - but they have been combined, giving them an average of 100 points, for the guest score for the BBC predictions league table.

Industry observers note that that means they miss out on the weekly win, which ended up in a tie between the BBC readers and AI. They both got six correct results with no exact scores, for a tally of 120 points.

There was only one game where everyone picked the right outcome - Liverpool's 3-1 win over Crystal Palace.

Chris, FM 27, Miles, AI and the BBC readers all backed the Reds to win, but AI was the only one to get the score spot on.

There were two games where no-one got the correct result - Nottingham Forest's win over Manchester City, and Sunderland's victory against Chelsea.

Out of more than 25,000 predictions, fewer than 1,500 people thought Forest would beat City and only 36 of them got the 3-1 scoreline right too.
