General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: How a green economy could help reverse climate change

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1443 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Human civilization is presently profoundly unsustainable.
  • If economies and societies keep to business as usual, the Earth's vital processes will continue to be thrown wildly out of balance, threatening the future of humanity.
  • Recent findings suggest that it's now largely accepted that if humans are to have any chance of slowing global warming and nature loss, those social and economic models must change.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Human civilization is presently profoundly unsustainable. Earth has already crossed seven of the nine planetary boundaries critical for sustaining life, including climate change, ocean acidification and biosphere integrity.

If economies and societies keep to business as usual, the Earth's vital processes will continue to be thrown wildly out of balance, threatening the future of humanity.

Recent findings suggest that it's now largely accepted that if humans are to have any chance of slowing global warming and nature loss, those social and economic models must change. That's where the idea of green growth comes in.

Its promise is to keep growing the economy while reducing emissions and resource use. That involves, for instance, running factories, businesses and homes on wind, solar and other green energy instead of coal and gas, replacing gas-fired furnaces with heat pumps and  recycling and reusing resources and raw materials.

"Basically, the idea is: business as usual, but with more sustainable technologies," stated Helmut Haberl, a social ecology professor at BOKU University in Vienna. Along with his colleagues, he published a major report in 2020 evaluating more than 800 studies on green growth.

In principle, the world's economic output could continue to grow in the long term and generate significantly fewer emissions from the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas. That's been shown in scenarios modeled by researchers with the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, or IPCC.

Thanks to renewable energy and green technologies, those scenarios have already become reality in several countries and regions.

According to recent reports, the economies of developed countries like the United Kingdom, the United States, Japanand Australia have experienced years of growth alongside sinking CO2 emissions. That's even when offshore production is included.

In the European Union, the bloc-wide economy has grown by more than 70% since 1990. Meanwhile, the EU's carbon emissions have dropped by around 40%.

But such a complete decoupling of growth and emissions is, according to Haberl and his fellow researchers, relatively rare.

It has been revealed that in India, and in several countries in Africa and Southeast Asia, economies are becoming more efficient. But while economic performance is outpacing emissions growth, emissions are still rising in those countries and globally. This is not compatible with preventing the worst impacts of climate change.

"That doesn't mean, however, that it couldn't work in the future," said Haberl, referring to decoupling of growth and emissions.

And even though economic growth has been shown to be compatible with emissions reduction, eliminating all greenhouse gases from a polluting industry like steel or chemicals is complicated.

These sectors don't just release emissions by burning fossil fuels for energy; carbon is also a key part of the chemical processes used to create their products, notably in the steel industry.

Replacing it with greener substitutes, or an alternative energy source like green hydrogen, requires significant investment.

It has been revealed that there's another hurdle: the world's high consumption of resources. A productive economy depends on many raw materials and other products: ores, chemicals, wood, cement, glass and agricultural products.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Many countries are now using green technologies to reduce the amount of resources needed to manufacture a product, for example, and are making their economies more efficient.

Industry observers note that but that doesn't mean overall fewer resources are being used because falling costs can encourage businesses to produce more things and people to consume more. This can partially offset green savings and is called the rebound effect.

The British economy has been growing for years, emissions have been dropping and efficiency has increased, but the UK still used 7% more resources in 2023 than it did in 2001.

Global resource consumption has tripled over the last 50 years. If the world continues on the current pathway, that could increase by another 60% by 2060. It remains unclear whether green growth can deliver the emissions and resource reductions needed to stop climate change and biodiversity loss rapidly enough.

"We really need to move beyond efficiency gains in our existing production practices to look more broadly at what we consume," mentioned Catherine Ganzleben, a sustainability and fair transitions expert at the European Environment Agency.

She told DW that people also need to reconsider how they consume and whether they really need to own everything they use in their daily life — cars, for example.

"But we can shift towards models where we share cars, so we pool our resources and have significantly lower resources per person through sharing the goods that we need.".

Some researchers have concluded that unrestricted economic growth is no longer possible in the long term, even if it's sustainable.

Instead, they've called for degrowth. This posits slower economic growth, no growth at all or even negative growth, so that the world's ecosystems and the climate have a chance to recover and stabilize.

That applies mainly to economies in richer countries, which would need to take targeted steps to reduce their energy and resource use. Poorer countries would continue to grow until their economies and quality of life improve significantly.

In a recent development, under the degrowth theory, a society's prosperity is not measured solely by the growth of its gross domestic product, but by values such as quality of life, education and community. The idea is that once countries develop to a certain point, additional growth doesn't translate into greater well-being.

Industry observers note that ultimately, the concept is based on the idea that human well-being and ecological sustainability is only possible in the long term with a planned, socially just reduction of material production and resource consumption. Degrowth advocates argue this would be preferable to an unplanned and potentially catastrophic economic contraction caused by escalating climate extremes.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

A 2020 study by researchers from the universities of Leeds and Lausanne demonstrated that the concept of degrowth supported the world's climate goals — and that a high quality of life didn't have to be sacrificed in exchange for a significantly lower consumption of energy and resources.

However, there is still no conclusive evidence that an entire modern economy could continue to function entirely on the degrowth principles in the long term.

Nevertheless, Haberl doesn't assume that an environmentally friendly economic model automatically goes hand in hand with sacrifice, arguing instead for a needs-based economy.

"A society isn't necessarily better off when it's producing more goods and services," he noted. It all depends on how prosperity and quality of life are measured in the future, and how states decide to do business.

Recent findings suggest that today, a successful economy is measured by the growth of a country's gross domestic product — put simply, the worth of all of its goods and services. This calculation doesn't account for income distribution, unpaid work, quality of life or environmental damage.

According to recent reports, "The highest possible real incomes for every individual would probably not be compatible with ecological goals in the long term," noted Haberl. "On the other hand, an increase in prosperity — related to a higher quality of life — would be.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that an analysis by the European Environment Agency (EEA) pointed out that the idea of steady growth is part of the world's economic cycle, and deeply anchored in our institutions, norms and societal discourse. The job market and tax system are also closely tied to gross domestic product growth. A shrinking economy would therefore require a fundamental shift in our way of thinking.

Recent findings suggest that countries face a dilemma: a steadily growing economy is not compatible with ecological goals, according to the EEA. On the other side, a sharp decline in growth could trigger enormous social upheaval.

Industry observers note that and the correlation is much more complex than the idea of "less is more," as highlighted by an EEA study in November 2021. "The fact that GDP growth has been harmful for the environment does not necessarily mean that declining GDP would be good for the environment," noted the report.

Recent findings suggest that achieving green growth while respecting environmental limits would require an "unprecedented decoupling of economic activity from environmental and climate pressures. Whether this is feasible is currently uncertain.".

This article was originally written in German.

  • After closing the largest initial public offering in history on Wednesday, Anthropic has about $200 billion in the bank, more than every tech giant besides Alphabet.
  • In a recent development, some financial analysts say that gap doesn’t look concerning when you factor in that the tech giant’s most recent quarterly sales were $17 billion, up more than 1,100 percent from the year before.
  • According to recent reports, the case for pessimism over the long term rests on problems that may slow Anthropic’s progress in developing new tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After closing the largest initial public offering in history on Wednesday, Anthropic has about $200 billion in the bank, more than every tech giant besides Alphabet. But the AI lab has also committed to paying vendors more than $900 billion over the next 19 years, mostly to develop data centers powering Claude and its other AI models.

In a recent development, some financial analysts say that gap doesn’t look concerning when you factor in that the tech giant’s most recent quarterly sales were $17 billion, up more than 1,100 percent from the year before. Anthropic shares, trading under the ticker symbol ANT, jumped more than 30 percent when they debuted on Nasdaq midday Thursday.

According to recent reports, the case for pessimism over the long term rests on problems that may slow Anthropic’s progress in developing new tools. This month, US voters largely rejected data centers when given the chance, and protests against new projects show no signs of slowing. Delays in the launch or expansion of new facilities could leave Anthropic struggling to train more powerful AI models.

“The jury’s still out on whether artificial intelligence is going to benefit everyone, or just a few people,” indicates Elaine Matheny, one of 70 members of Mason County United, a grassroots organization fighting an under-construction data center intended for Anthropic in West Virginia. “Do we really need to cover up all our farmland so Claude can do all our thinking for us?”.

Sources indicate that then there are the concerns about the safety and security of Anthropic’s models. At a livestreamed investor meeting last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei noted developing safeguards was the limiting factor in deploying its AI models. “We don’t want these agents to run wild,” he said. It’s possible the firm could prioritize safety to a point that stunts growth.

The San Francisco-based developer is organized as a public benefit corporation, a legal designation that allows it to prioritize societal impacts alongside shareholder interests. Amodei has mentioned the tech giant held back a new model earlier this year, jeopardizing sales to protect the public from potentially harmful technology. He also has said the company tries to screen for hires “oriented toward the public benefit” to ingrain the safety culture among its 5,300 employees, which is “painful in the short run” as the company passes over otherwise qualified candidates.

In a recent development, anthropic’s market debut is the largest for a so-called PBC, and the first for a manufacturer solely focused on generative AI development. It also represents a triumph for the handful of renegade engineers and business leaders who started it. They siphoned themselves off from OpenAI in the midst of the pandemic nearly six years ago over strategic differences, and the two companies have been rivals ever since.

For some time, OpenAI was expected to go public first, but executive departures, shifting priorities, and legal troubles have introduced roadblocks.

Anthropic also has some compelling numbers to show investors. Revenue is soaring, while operating losses are declining. Its massive spat with the US Department of Defense this year over limits on Claude use doesn’t appear to have significantly slowed growth. Overall, the number of customers spending six figures annually is up 12 times compared to a year ago. “I don’t think you could have dreamt of an [IPO prospectus] that’s as good,” indicates Tomasz Tunguz, general partner at the investment firm Theory Ventures.

It has been revealed that because of how Anthropic must account for compensating employees with stock, it’s still wildly unprofitable—over $104 billion in losses this year through September. That’s no matter when investors are eager to buy shares and lend money.

The IPO raised about $81 billion (more than $107 billion when adding in private sales of shares), which is more than the $75 billion SpaceX received in June in a previous world record. Anthropic’s initial valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion fell short of SpaceX’s nearly $1.8 trillion, though the Elon Musk-led rocket maker does have a more sprawling business beyond AI. (OpenAI has been valued at $1.25 trillion in an ongoing fundraising campaign.).

Anthropic reportedly sought, but failed, to achieve a higher valuation, suggesting some anxiety on Wall Street. US midterm election results have increased the possibility of fresh regulations on emerging technologies. Fears about the debt enabling AI data center development are rising, and a potential pullback in investment from Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang’s sudden exit are deepening those worries.

Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have insisted investors are bullish in the long term because demand for AI models is surging. But it’s questionable whether the companies can sustain their business without coming up with ever more powerful models that drive their profits by enabling customers to automate upcoming types of work. Without eye-catching capabilities, customers could shift to cheaper alternatives.

In a recent development, some Anthropic employees have taken the safety concerns to extremes. Researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic in September, citing a belief that humanity could be destroyed within a couple of years without even more focus on keeping models under human control. But, more recently, Coxon was quoted by the Stanford Daily as saying that he might return to Anthropic because he suspects he could have “more of an impact” working on safety there.

Industry observers note that notably, Amodei mentioned safety as a challenge even above access to electricity for data centers, which many other AI companies list as their top concern. On the ground, people opposing data centers have griped about not just higher power bills, but also construction-induced traffic and housing woes, environmental pollution, and a lack of significant financial benefit.

At data center developer Nscale’s site for Anthropic in West Virginia, extreme rain combined with grading (leveling or sloping ground for construction) coincided with flooding in neighbor’s backyards. “We’re frustrated, we’re angry,” the community spokesperson Matheny says. “We want [data centers] in more logical locations and not to be considering profit as the only guideline.” (Nscale says it has fixed damage and bought out some homeowners at above-market rates.).

Environmental activists have pointed out that Anthropic has made no commitment about using renewable power at its data centers, and has never published an environmental impact report.

Sources indicate that “Clearly permitting a latest data center development will be extremely difficult in the US,” Tunguz notes. Pushback could force Anthropic and others to focus outside the US for data centers. That will add risk, complexity, and cost, he says.

A handful of labor groups and others including National Nurses United urged retirement funds to steer clear of the IPO, saying they “should not be invested in companies that harm our communities and allow a handful of individuals to accumulate historic fortunes and power.”.

Yolanda Daniel, a member of the homeowner associations’ coalition Environmental Advocates Mississippi, says Anthropic is socializing the cost of AI development and privatizing the gains from it. “That is not how a public benefit corporation operates,” she says, vowing to do everything she can to stop next year’s planned opening of an Anthropic data center across the street from her.

Recent findings suggest that anthropic’s IPO paperwork argued some of its public benefit will materialize as employees and early investors become some of the world’s biggest philanthropists. But there’s no guarantee of that, or that anyone will give away their money to causes that directly benefit disgruntled communities. And if employees donate shares to one of the philanthropic funds the manufacturer offers, they also consolidate power with Amodei by handing over their voting rights to him.

Amodei and his fellow cofounders collectively hold a majority of Anthropic’s shareholder voting power. Some investor watchdogs have warned about what they view as concentrated control. But a successful debut has shown investors are entrusting Amodei and his associates with building the biggest organization in the world—that is if he can find the employees and data centers to do it.

Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bruno Guimarães to feel the heat on Tyneside, Alex Scott’s return further cheers Cherries and Manchester City face favourite whipping boys.
  • After three Premier League defeats on the spin, Manchester City need something or someone to come along and put some pep in their step, and Fulham look like just the thing – after all, in the past 15 years these teams have played 20 times in all competitions, and City have won precisely 20 of those games.
  • Manchester City v Fulham, Saturday 12.30pm (all times GMT).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bruno Guimarães to feel the heat on Tyneside, Alex Scott’s return further cheers Cherries and Manchester City face favourite whipping boys.

After three Premier League defeats on the spin, Manchester City need something or someone to come along and put some pep in their step, and Fulham look like just the thing – after all, in the past 15 years these teams have played 20 times in all competitions, and City have won precisely 20 of those games. Their current run of 17 successive league wins against Fulham is the longest run of victories by one club against a single opponent in English top-flight history. It is a reflection of the changing realities of English football, and the gulf that has opened between the teams that dominate it and those who seek to challenge them, that of the top 10 such runs all but one occurred in whole or in part after 2010 and six of them have been achieved by Sheikh Mansour’s Manchester City, with Chelsea responsible for another two, Manchester United one, and Portsmouth’s postwar, 13-game supremacy over Everton – a wild ride that included two 5-0s, a 5-1, a 6-3 and a 7-0 – the anomaly. Simon Burnton.

Manchester City v Fulham, Saturday 12.30pm (all times GMT).

Positivity surrounds Aston Villa despite them failing to win in four matches, the last of which ended in agonising fashion; they had to settle for a 4-4 draw at Manchester United after twice squandering a two-goal advantage. Villa should have managed the final minutes better, but a home date with Sunderland presents an opportunity to return to winning ways. Unai Emery needs to eliminate the defensive naivety that has blighted some performances and the expected absence of Matty Cash, this time owing to concussion sustained on Poland duty, would deny the Villa manager his preferred defensive lineup. This fixture threw up a classic last season, Tammy Abraham scoring a stoppage-time winner to extend the visitors’ miserable record at Villa Park. Sunderland have won on only two of their past 17 league visits, their last victory coming in 2011 courtesy of the former Villa loanee Phil Bardsley. Ben Fisher.

Aston Villa v Sunderland, Saturday 3pm.

The last time Alex Scott played for Bournemouth, Marco Rose was yet to taste victory in the Premier League. When the 23-year-old returns to midfield he will do so with the team in a totally different place. Bournemouth have racked up eight straight wins in all competitions before hosting Nottingham Forest on Saturday and Scott, who has been able to build his fitness during the international break after a thigh problem, may have to wait his turn owing to the form of Tyler Adams and Ryan Christie. If Rose opts for momentum, then Eli Junior Kroupi, fresh from scoring his first France goal, could make his first start of the season after sustaining a freak foot injury in pre-season. Bournemouth have hardly been short of firepower, though, with Evanilson scoring seven goals in his past eight games. BF.

Bournemouth v Nottingham Forest, Saturday 3pm.

Chelsea left Wearside battered and bruised after being pushed around by Brian Brobbey. The Sunderland forward bullied Wesley Fofana and Levi Colwill, who had to be substituted at half-time, and won the game’s decisive penalty with a solo run that left Xabi Alonso angry with his side’s powderpuff defending. Alonso insisted Chelsea had prepared for Brobbey’s threat; the Chelsea manager will hope they are better at putting the plan into practice when they face another target man on Saturday. Leeds head to Stamford Bridge and will look to Dominic Calvert-Lewin, fresh from helping England get over the line against Spain last weekend, to unnerve Alonso’s defenders. Jacob Steinberg.

According to recent reports, thomas Frank’s first assessment of his newly introduced charges after taking over at Crystal Palace this week included the nuggets that “we’re conceding too many goals … we need to work on the defensive side of things with principles, attitude, everything regarding that”, and in particular “we need to work on the set pieces, that’s key”. If he can’t inspire an immediate improvement this is where this match could be decided, being as it is an encounter between the league’s worst set-piece defenders – no one comes close to the 67 shots and xG of 7.44 coughed up by Palace at restarts – and the best. Though Coventry have let in one goal from set pieces, and neither Brentford nor Liverpool have shipped any, the hosts’ set-piece xG of 1.65 is a league low, and they were equally outstanding from dead-ball situations in the Championship last season. The home side will be boosted by the return of the 6ft 4in defender Bobby Thomas, who, despite a calf injury that meant he missed the last two games and the final third of the one before that, has still made more clearances than any other Coventry player. SB.

Coventry v Crystal Palace, Saturday 3pm.

It has been revealed that it may have been a slightly strange week for Tottenham fans. They have watched as their former managers Mauricio Pochettino and Thomas Frank have been installed at Manchester United and Crystal Palace respectively, while their current head coach, Roberto De Zerbi, picked up the Premier League’s manager of the month award for October. That is reflective of the improvement De Zerbi has overseen in recent weeks, with Spurs happy to move forward with the Italian and avoid the chaos enveloping some of their rivals. The long-held assumption among some connected to Tottenham that Pochettino would one day return to save the club must now be banished; De Zerbi needs full buy-in from everyone to build his project. That’s the only way Spurs can ensure they steer clear of future crises. Dominic Booth.

Tottenham v Ipswich, Saturday 3pm.

Industry observers note that with the temperature in Newcastle forecast to dip to 0C at kick-off, Matthias Jaissle is perhaps hoping that his team’s guests from north London (where a balmy 9C is predicted at 5.30pm) freeze in the Tyneside chill. Otherwise it is hard to envisage his young side overcoming a formidable looking Arsenal on a day when Newcastle’s head coach seeks what would be only his second win in seven games. Home fans will not merely be hurt by the sight of their much-missed former captain Bruno Guimarães wearing Arsenal colours but decidedly nervous about a fixture that precedes a run of tricky engagements involving a trip to Brighton and home dates with Manchester United and Sunderland. Jaissle’s cause could be helped should Mikel Arteta name Guimarães in his starting XI and the crowd respond to the once adored Brazilian’s defection by creating the sort of hostile atmosphere that might just galvanise a Newcastle team expected to contain the former Arsenal midfielder Joe Willock. Meanwhile Jaissle’s defence must be mindful of the threat posed by another Newcastle old boy in Mikel Merino. Louise Taylor.

Newcastle v Arsenal, Saturday 5.30pm.

Sources indicate that brighton are out to prove their early-season form has been no fluke and the fixture list for November and December looks promising for their chances of retaining their lofty position. Hull, having started the season with back-to-back league victories, now appear vulnerable and have not won since that August burst. Brighton follow the trip to Humberside with a home game against Universitatea Craiova in the Conference League, then host Newcastle, and face none of the major six until a visit to Tottenham on 29 December. With Brighton having won seven of their 10 league games, tentative talk of a title challenge may not seem so fanciful come Christmas. The challenge tactically for Fabian Hürzeler’s men will be to deal with the tag of favourites for most of their upcoming games, with teams perhaps starting to wise up to Brighton’s high-pressing, vertical style. DB.

Recent findings suggest that and so it starts all over again. Manchester United’s eighth permanent manager in 13 years – not forgetting the interim spells of Ryan Giggs, Michael Carrick, Ralf Rangnick, Ruud van Nistelrooy and Darren Fletcher – was impressively quick to commit to the cause when taking a private jet from Cincinnati to Manchester immediately after his final game as USA head coach. Mauricio Pochettino needs his fresh, floundering team to reciprocate at Anfield. United have conceded four times in the first four minutes of a game this season, seven goals in the opening 17 minutes in total, and will have had little time to absorb instructions from their latest coach by the time they face an expectant Liverpool. United’s defensive options might tempt many managers to board the next flight out but, as a decent record against the so-called big six since the start of last season demonstrates, the team are capable of showing up when they feel like it. That is just one of the many issues Pochettino has to address. Andy Hunter.

Liverpool v Manchester United, Sunday 4.30pm.

In a recent development, fans of neutral officiating will appreciate the fact that both Brentford and Everton have won six games refereed by Craig Pawson, who will take charge of this match. But where the two clubs’ experiences diverge is that, while Brentford have only danced to the tune of the Pawson whistle 12 times, enjoying a 50% win ratio, Everton have toiled through 33 Pawson-helmed matches for an equivalent figure of 18%. Of Everton’s past 14 Pawson-patrolled matches there has been only one victory, and 10 defeats. Pawson, meanwhile, has taken charge of five Brentford home matches and they have won every one, thanks in part to the two penalties he has awarded them (both converted), compared with the one he gave against them (missed). Jack Grealish is back having sat out Everton’s past four league games because of illness, lack of fitness and a breach of club discipline, but given that, of the three Premier League matches he has missed, Everton won the two most recent – and the other one was at Arsenal – he may not go straight back into the team. Indeed of Everton’s four league wins this season, Grealish has missed three and played only eight minutes in a fourth. SB.

Brentford v Everton, Monday 8pm.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After a full season of cutthroat legal proceedings, War's central divorce trial between actor Carla Duval (Sienna Miller) and tech mogul Morgan Henderson (Dominic West) has reached its final verdict. The winner? No one. But the loser? Also no one.

Sources indicate that that's because, after some eleventh-hour heroics from mole Johnny Warren (Archie Renaux) and honeypot Flora Monroe (Rose Williams), Carla and Morgan reach their own settlement, independent of their lawyers and the judge. Following their decision, Carla will receive 50 percent of Zephyr's shares and monthly payments from Morgan until he retires. Carla and Morgan will share custody of Carla's son, Gabe (Aran Murphy). In short, it's basically what Carla had been asking for this whole time, and what the pair could have achieved without going to court.

Recent findings suggest that their decision stems from hearing Flora read Morgan's conciliatory letter to Carla, which St. John Smallwood (Pip Torrens) tried to dispose of, aloud in court. For Carla and Morgan, the letter is a reminder of the good in their relationship, something they sorely needed to recall after months of highly public mud-slinging.

In a recent development, "It tied itself up with humanity and kindness, and that was unexpected for me when I was reading it," Miller told Mashable in a junket interview alongside West. "I think the moral of that being that had these two people dropped their ego and their pride and nasty covetousness, if they'd let all of that go, they could have probably resolved this without the hideous experience of taking each other to court.".

"It felt like a spectacular waste of $10 million on lawyers' fees," West joked.

For series creator George Kay, there was never a version of War Season 1 where the court ruled in favor of one side or the other.

Recent findings suggest that "In the majority of these significant divorces, the real winners are the lawyers, and so we wanted to take that agency away from the justice system and put it back in the hands of [Carla and Morgan]," Kay told Mashable in a junket interview. "So, it was always going to be down to them to work it out, which is the big expensive irony of what they've been through.".

By the end of Season 1, Carla and Morgan have found what seems to be an affectionate alliance. Even though Carla now has the Zephyr shares she asked for, she won't be using them against Morgan to trigger the sale to Michael Ancker (David Menkin), as Zephyr CEO Gillian Pope (Angel Coulby) wanted. Instead, Gillian is being ousted, as it turns out she leaked the security footage of Flora leaving Morgan's hotel room to the press.

In War's final scene between Carla and Morgan, the pair stand, at peace, on a Normandy beach by their cottage.

"I'll always love you," Morgan tells Carla.

In a recent development, as it seems that the pair is about to go their separate ways, Carla calls Morgan back up to the cottage for a hot chocolate with Gabe. It's proof that their life as a pairing isn't over. It's just taken a different shape. And maybe thanks to that, both Carla and Morgan "won" in the trial after all.

"The end of a divorce, it's not like someone's dead," West remarked. "You either never speak to each other again, run screaming through the streets, or you realize actually why you love the person in the first place. I think that's what happens to Morgan in the end.".

In a recent development, "We described this divorce at the world's most expensive couples therapy, because it's only by going through everything that they've been through, hearing what the other one thinks via their lawyers, emotionally reengaging with everything they've had in their relationship, that by the end they realize what an amazing thing they have, and so we leave them okay," Kay stated. "They're divorced, technically, but actually they're much better parents and they're much closer emotionally, and that was always a North Star for us.".

The sweet ending for Morgan and Carla is at odds with the rest of War's bloodthirsty, win-at-any-cost tone. But for Kay, that was intentional.

Industry observers note that "We didn't want it to be bleak or dark," Kay said of the ending. "We wanted it to be redemptive.".

'A shotgun marriage': Why are NASA's SkyFall Mars helicopters riding on a nuclear rocket?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1483 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The pace is picking up on building, testing, and plotting out the flight paths for a trio of NASA Ingenuity-class helicopters to investigate Mars after riding there on a nuclear-powered rocket.
  • In a recent development, NASA's Skyfall mission will see those mini-choppers dropped off at Mars by the space agency's Space Reactor-1 Freedom (SR-1) rocket, the first fission nuclear-powered interplanetary spacecraft slated for launch in late 2028.
  • But some experts are questioning why NASA is combining two such high-profile missions into one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The pace is picking up on building, testing, and plotting out the flight paths for a trio of NASA Ingenuity-class helicopters to investigate Mars after riding there on a nuclear-powered rocket.

In a recent development, NASA's Skyfall mission will see those mini-choppers dropped off at Mars by the space agency's Space Reactor-1 Freedom (SR-1) rocket, the first fission nuclear-powered interplanetary spacecraft slated for launch in late 2028. After its cruise phase and initial Mars flyby in 2029, that nuclear carrier craft will make a second Mars approach in the Fall of 2030 to unleash a SkyFall entry capsule outfitted with a fleet of small aerial vehicles that will soar across the Red Planet.

But some experts are questioning why NASA is combining two such high-profile missions into one. "It is clear that SkyFall was approved for programmatic or political reasons," said Scott Hubbard, former director of NASA's Ames Research Center and the first Mars Program Director (aka the "Mars Czar") at NASA Headquarters, told Space.com. "The connection to Space Reactor-1 seems to me to be a bit of a shotgun marriage, a tech-demo piggybacking on another mission as an opening bid for a 'nuclear NASA.'".

In a recent development, hubbard is a retired adjunct professor of aeronautics and astronautics at Stanford University. He is a major voice in shaping Red Planet exploration goals, drawing upon his expertise as NASA's former foremost Mars authority. His understanding is that the basic concept had been developed as a follow on to Ingenuity, an attempt to move beyond a technology demo and into a science platform.

Hubbard said that combining these two observations, the outcome presents "an unusual set of management challenges." Since the SkyFall mission concept first appeared, he said, the usual sequence for a science mission is reversed.

Industry observers note that "The science community is having to scramble to back into a set of requirements and objectives that match the SkyFall capabilities. Fortunately the community is very creative," mentioned Hubbard, "and the basic Planetary Decadal objectives are very broad.".

Decadal surveys reflect a broad consensus within the scientific community and provide detailed insights into the strategic priorities and mission directives set for the next decade across key scientific domains, including planetary exploration.

However, Hubbard said he has heard griping about the "fait accompli" process, "but the planetary community will make lemonade.".

It should be noted however, Hubbard continued, that this process is not how you would design a strategic set of missions as precursors for human exploration.

"SR-1 Freedom is a technology demo that may or may not be ready for the Mars launch window in 2028. It is clear that the Mars Program has a standard launch concept in their back pocket," said Hubbard. "Nuclear Electric Propulsion [NEP] is of little value in traveling to Mars, not shaving any time off the transit. The real value of NEP is for risk reduction, use at the moon, outer planets and even bolder ideas like interstellar travel," Hubbard concluded.

"This, by far, is the shortest Mars mission ever conceived of," remarked Matthew Golombek, SkyFall Project Scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif., speaking Nov. 10 during the virtual meeting of the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group (MEPAG).

According to recent reports, kick-started by NASA in March 2026, the SkyFall project has grown from roughly six people to over 200 individuals who are now working on the initiative, said Golombek. "This is an incredibly rapid development and build," he said.

"It's really to demonstrate that exploration is possible with helicopters … filling what I call a 'resolution gap' between orbital information and surface information," Golombek told the MEPAG.

In a recent development, once deployed by a helicopter deployment system, the threesome will spin up their rotors at about a kilometer above the surface of Mars. Then each helicopter lands on its own, ready to undertake flights every other solar day on the Red Planet. On average, a day (labeled as a sol) on Mars lasts 24 hours 39 minutes 35 seconds, from one noon to the next.

SkyFall's prime mission is six months, with a one-year goal," Golombek mentioned, and the intent is to arrive in northern spring on Mars, a time where the vehicles are unlikely to encounter dust storms.

On the to-do list of NASA level one science requisites are for the helicopters to capture high-resolution imagery, perform a set scientific tasks, and help to prepare for future human exploration of Mars, said Golombek.

Industry observers note that from their initial landing spots, the whirlybirds could potentially go tens to 100's of kilometers or more in different directions. Identical for all three helicopters, the nominal payload consists of five instruments, plus engineering navigation cameras.

That gear can examine the subsurface structure of Mars, the geomorphology and geology of surface terrains, as well as look at the meteorology of the atmosphere and the planet's radiation environment.

"The real star of the show is ground penetrating radar [GPR] with a flexible antenna," Golombek noted. That ultra-small GPR hardware can look for buried rocks, the layering of the Mars home turf, as well as spot subsurface ice deposits.

"If you have this aerial access and the ability to scout ahead," Golombek noted, "you would go a long way towards better defining where to go with a rover and what kind of more detailed surface studies to do with subsequent missions.".

Sources indicate that all that stated, yet to be plotted out are science-focused traverses for the SkyFall helicopters. But there are early ideas.

"The real kicker is that these spacecraft are the smallest landers ever attempted on Mars," mentioned Golombek. "You are looking for a place that virtually has no rocks," he pointed out, a must-have to assure high probability of landing safely. So toss in for good measure low surface slopes, no major craters, a site not overloaded with dust.

One early idea is to revisit the crash locales of discarded SkyFall descent hardware – fuel tanks, cruise stage and associated gear – equipment large and heavy enough to survive entry, smack into the Mars landscape and high-speed and generate craters.

Sources indicate that "So if there is ice at centimeters depth, we would create our own icy impact craters," Golombek mentioned. "We could actually visit them in a time-scale before the ice actually sublimates," he said.

Another site getting the eye, albeit deemed a design reference target but considered a "pretty good spot," is within Arcadia Planitia in Mars's northern lowlands. Studies have indicated the presence of substantial volumes of near-surface excess ice there.

Sources indicate that "There is a vast amount of information to suggest large quantities of regional ice deposits at that location," stated Golombek. "This is at least one location that appears to meet all the engineering constraints and would be a potentially safe landing site…virtually no rocks," he advised.

According to recent reports, in the past, Golombek added, JPL took part in SpaceX-sponsored workshops to look for ice deposits as close to the equator of Mars that could be found. Arcadia Planitia was flagged as superior Starship touchdown terrain.

In a recent development, "Most of the landing sites considered for humans have talked about going to places with ice deposits. Ice provides both a consumable as well as fuel to get back off the planet," said Golombek.

For the near-term, scientific community input next year — via two workshops — are on tap, reviewing the science of SkyFall and also help sort out potential landing sites for final decision-making at NASA Headquarters.

Meanwhile, as SkyFall literally spins up, there is the need for on-time delivery of Space Reactor-1 Freedom.

Golombek remarked NASA considers the two endeavors as a pair.

"If SR-1 is not ready, SkyFall could be rolled out on any conventional launch vehicle without any difficulty whatsoever," said Golombek, "something like a Falcon 9 would be more than sufficient, but others are possible as well.".

He also wrote "Mars: Our Future on the Red Planet" released in 2016 by National Geographic. Leonard  has served as a correspondent for SpaceNews, Scientific American and Aerospace America for the AIAA. #13335. Voyager Is a Light-Day Away. Here’s How Far That Really Is

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1375 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Voyager Is a Light-Day Away. Here’s How Far That Really Is

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1375 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Voyager 1 spacecraft rolled out from Earth in September 1977.
  • It’s not just old; it’s also really far away.
  • According to recent reports, the expanse separating it from Earth raises so many interesting physics questions about Voyager 1’s epic, well, voyage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Voyager 1 spacecraft rolled out from Earth in September 1977.

It’s not just old; it’s also really far away. In fact, it’s so far that it takes light one whole day to travel from the spacecraft to Earth and vice versa. That puts its distance at one light-day.

According to recent reports, the expanse separating it from Earth raises so many interesting physics questions about Voyager 1’s epic, well, voyage. Let’s get to the questions—and the answers.

Sources indicate that in science, we like to measure things, including distance. Surely, you’re familiar with meters. If you put a mass on a string and let it swing back and forth (like the pendulum of a clock), it will take about 1 second to go from side to side if the string is 1 meter long.

In a recent development, but if you want to measure larger distances like the proximity of stuff in space, this unit swiftly becomes silly because objects are so far apart. While kilometers can be helpful for measuring the distance between things like Earth and the International Space Station or the moon, even they become hard to comprehend at larger scales.

Enter the Astronomical Unit, or AU, which is the average distance from the sun to the Earth, or about 1.5 x 1011 meters. Humans found this distance by observing the transit of Venus. This transit is like a solar eclipse, except instead of the moon passing in front of the sun, it’s the planet Venus. Looking at Venus’ movement from different locations on Earth, the planet creates a shadow at different times. If you know the radius of the Earth, you can find this distance from the Earth to sun.

But what if you want to measure the distance to a star outside the solar system? AUs start to become a little unwieldy. Enter the parsec. No matter what Han Solo indicates in Star Wars, the parsec is a unit of distance and not the best time for the Kessel Run.

And it’s a long distance: for comparison, 1 parsec is about 200,000 AUs. The parsec is a way to measure distance using parallax. You can get the mechanics of parallax by holding your thumb out with an extended arm in front of your face. Close one eye and line up your thumb with an object across the room. Now close that eye and open your other eye. You will notice that the thumb seems to shift its position. The size of the angular shift depends on both the distance between observation locations—the distance between your eyes—and the distance to the object. The farther the object, the less parallax shift you will observe.

According to recent reports, as Earth orbits the sun, we have different observation locations while looking at stars. Imagine an observation shift of 1 AU (you would get a 2 AU shift going from December to June). If a star has a parallax shift of 1 arc-second, we say it has a distance of 1 parsec.

Industry observers note that at one point, astronomer Friedrich Bessel was using parallax to measure the distance to a star. He said that it was so far away that it would take light 10.3 years to reach the Earth. Boom, there’s your unit of distance, the light-year. It’s the distance light travels in one year, or 9.9 x 1015 meters, or over 6 million AU. But we can use any unit of time to measure distance with light. One light-day is the distance that light travels in 24 hours, or 2.6 x 1013 meters. That’s really far. In fact, no human-made object has gone farther. Let’s say that Voyager traveled at a constant speed and in a straight line (it didn’t). That would give it an average speed of 164 kilometers per second or about 36,000 mph.

In a recent development, voyager has felt a lot of different forces out in space. The first is the rockets that got it there. But let’s talk about the other ones it has encountered.

First, there’s gravitational force. There is an attractive gravitational force between any two objects with mass. The force depends on the masses of the two objects and the distance between them. The force is there on any number of scales: Since your body has a mass (maybe around 70 kilograms) and your phone has a mass (about 200 grams), there is an attractive force. If the phone is about 50 centimeters from your body, the gravitational force the phone exerts on you is about 4 x 10-9 newtons. In other words, it’s exceedingly tiny. (Depending on how much you love your phone, though, the attraction may feel stronger.).

Industry observers note that for Voyager, there’s also a gravitational interaction with masses—like the outer planets it was originally introduced to observe, as well as Earth. However, the really big gravitational influence is from the sun, since it has such a large mass (2 x 1030 kilograms). Using the mass of Voyager 1 at 722 kilograms, there is an attractive force of 1.4 x 10-4 newtons. That’s equivalent to the weight of 78 grains of salt on the surface of the Earth.

The only other object that would have a substantial relationship to Voyager 1 is the planet Jupiter, with a mass of 1.9 x 1027 kilograms. But it’s only when Voyager was fairly close to the planet way back in 1979 that this gravitational force would even partially compare to the interaction with the sun.

Recent findings suggest that there are other, more exotic interactions with the spacecraft, but these forces are also tiny. Solar winds—charged particles emitted from the surface of the sun—have blown past Voyager. Although they travel very fast, the mass of these particles is extremely small. The further you get from the sun, the more their intensity decreases as well.

The venerable craft is also likely to feel the impacts of magnetic fields and other weird things as it moves from a region where the primary interactions are with the sun—the heliosphere—to interactions with other stars and stuff—the interstellar medium.

It has been revealed that newton’s second law of motion says that forces on an object change its motion. As an equation, we can write this as net force = mass times acceleration. The acceleration is defined as the time rate of change of the velocity.

Let’s take the average speed we calculated above of 164 kilometers per second for simplicity’s sake. Does this velocity change? Yes. Remember, we calculated the gravitational force from the sun with a value of 1.4 x 10-4 newtons. To further simplify things, let’s assume that’s the only force acting on Voyager. Using that and the mass of the spacecraft, we get an acceleration of around 2 x 10-7 newtons. Since the gravitational force is mostly in the opposite direction as the motion of the spacecraft, though, this translates to a very slight deceleration. In one day of travel, Voyager 1 will only slow down by 0.012 meters per second.

Not much on a daily basis, but the craft does indeed slow down. Will this eventually make it stop? Actually, no. Remember, Voyager is moving away from the sun. That means that while it slows down a bit every day, it’s also getting farther from the sun and its gravitational force—the very thing slowing it down in the first place.

Industry observers note that it’s possible for an object to always slow down but never stop, and it will “escape” from the sun. Perhaps it’s not surprising that we call this the escape velocity. For the location of the Voyager, it needs to have a speed of at least 3.2 kilometers per second. If Voyager were slower, it would essentially “fall” back to the sun, just like an apple tossed in the air falls back to the Earth.

Industry observers note that of course, there are always things out there that could unexpectedly impact Voyager 1. Even a very tiny amount of interstellar dust will eventually slow it down further and perhaps even stop it. Or who knows, maybe it will become self-aware and turn into the V’Ger from Star Trek: The Motion Picture. Only time will tell.

The male footballers best associated with each shirt number – the readers’ edition

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that last week we selected 50 players who are synonymous with their squad numbers.
  • It has been revealed that which footballers are inextricably linked to their shirt numbers?
  • Sources indicate that an honourable mention should go to Aberdeen’s No 0.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that last week we selected 50 players who are synonymous with their squad numbers. Our readers spotted notable absentees so came up with an alternative list, which does not start at No 1 or end at No 50.

It has been revealed that which footballers are inextricably linked to their shirt numbers? We picked out 50 players last week who have come to embody the numbers on their backs. It was not an exhaustive list – as our readers have proved. We couldn’t include some legends of the game – Pelé and Lionel Messi for a start – and we missed a few brilliant stories. Thankfully our readers have provided an alternative list. And, creative bunch that they are, they have begun with No 0 and ended with No 51 ….

Sources indicate that an honourable mention should go to Aberdeen’s No 0. Zerouali is one of the very few to have worn the number (before rules were changed in Scotland). He was a cult hero during a poor time at the club, who died tragically young in a car crash. Lewis.

Sources indicate that the Manchester City No 1 in the 1940s, 1950s and 1960s. Your article said that Lev Yashin was an automatic choice for No 1. While mention was made of other goalkeepers, there was no nod in the direction of the great Bert Trautmann, the German prisoner of war who became a Manchester City legend. Yashin himself said “my only equal is the German boy at Manchester City”.

Bert’s goalkeeping achievements were many. He only started playing as a keeper in a prisoner of war team before signing for St Helens in the Lancashire Combination League on release from prison. A year later he signed for City, where he made more than 500 appearances as well as playing the last 17 minutes of the 1956 FA Cup final with a broken neck in the days before substitutes were allowed, making key saves towards the end to ensure a City victory. He was also the first goalkeeper voted Footballer of the Year.

Perhaps most remarkable of all, he saved 60% of penalties he faced. Unfortunately, he was not given any international recognition. As a German citizen he could not play for England and could only play for Germany if playing in the country. He would have been a certain starter in the Germany team that won the World Cup in 1954.

It has been revealed that he also did as much as anyone to repair British-German relations after the second world war. He went from being booed by 20,000 people on his City debut to being feted by more than 50,000 fans at his 1964 testimonial. He was awarded an honorary OBE in 2004. David Cronin.

According to recent reports, the greatest living Englishman; the best left-back to have played the game; the best player Nottingham Forest have ever had; and my hero (and Paolo Maldini’s). Will Kitchen.

The captain who drove Leeds forwards for well over a decade. Captain of club and country, Bremner was the human personification of Don Revie’s team of the 1960s and 1970s. He had skill, drive, aggression, camaraderie and he played close to (and over?) the line. Thirty years after his early death, he is still the player who Leeds fans hold up as representing the qualities they value in players. It is fitting that the only player to come close to him while wearing the white No 4 was another diminutive, copper-haired Scotsman, Gordon Strachan. As the wee Scotsman with the statue outside Elland Road remarked: “Side before self, every time.” Nick Ramage.

Stan Cullis, the Wolves manager at the time, converted Wright from wing-half to centre-half. He was little more than 5ft 8in, which suggests he would not be a good fit in the position, but he could jump and time it right. He captained England and was the first footballer in the world to gain 100 caps. He also captained Wolves and led them to some headline victories, most notably against Honved. Most importantly of all: he represents football before 1960, when football was more open, more exciting and more rapid in the transition. Kevin R Cox.

It has been revealed that he was the greatest ever No 6. If Pelé described him as the best defender he ever played against, how can the Guardian not choose him? He excelled at timing, passing and the ability to read a game. He also inspired West Ham and England with his presence. Tim Evans.

There are still a few of us left who had the great pleasure to see the greatest No 7 of all time play, for Blackpool and Stoke City. His return to Stoke in the 1960s rejuvenated a team that had been stuck in the Second Division for a long time and helped put them back where they belonged, in the top flight. Matthews was the greatest No 7 of his day and, I would suggest, of all time. John Heath.

I never saw him play but my father extolled his virtues to me. In this day and age when players are well paid, maybe overpaid, there should be a remembrance of those who went before them and created this wonderful game we call football. Nick Johnson.

In a recent development, so neither of the two greatest players to play the game, at least in my lifetime, is included. If we are talking about the beautiful game, then either Pelé (my preference) or Messi has to be the No 10. Richard Hirst.

Simply one of the best Premier League players this decade. His number 11 was often seen from behind, with the three defenders he was about to bamboozle looking worried in the background. Joe.

Keane was the most iconic and influential No 16. In the era of omnipresent Manchester United pundits, it’s easy to focus on the contemporary theatrical Keane playing the disgruntled, unimpressed one in the studio so well. But don’t lose sight of Keane winning duels, covering every blade of grass and spraying un-Hollywood but massively effective balls forward. Think Stadio delle Alpi, the scene where he tamed Zinedine Zidane and mounted a comeback against Juventus that enabled the Treble and all that. Think Lansdowne Road in 2001 when he essentially knocked out the Netherlands from the 2002 World Cup. Does Rodri have a movie with Steve Coogan in it? Michael Craig.

While I like Iván Zamorano and his little plus sign, Klinsmann wore 18 for much longer. He won the World Cup and European Championship (as captain) in it. He also decided to continue wearing it when No 9 was available, which Zamorano never did. Jochen.

The number was initially forced upon him at Eibar, but he kept it at Valencia because it meant following in the footsteps of Pablo Aimar. He disproved the received wisdom that shorter, “weaker”, technical players who sparkled in the Italian and Spanish leagues would not cope with the physicality of football in England. His tactical intelligence and impeccable technique were emblematic of the change in European football that was becoming impossible for English teams to ignore.

He was one of the key components of Manchester City’s all-conquering team, but he represents more than that: the move to a positional game; conserving and recycling possession as a means of placing pressure on the opponents; building up from the back, enabled by an offensive technical player dropping deep. These innovations would have reached the English game anyway, but his presence provided some initial familiarity with them.

He made 125 appearances for Spain, scoring 35 goals and providing 29 assists. He also guided Real Sociedad into a successful spell in his mid-30s. Toby.

His shirt number was retired when he moved to Borussia Dortmund and became, at the time, the most expensive 17-year-old in history. I’ve had the privilege of seeing two of Birmingham City’s greats – Trevor Francis will always be my No 8 shirt – putting seasoned defenders on their backsides or scoring brilliant goals. Francis and Bellingham were, and are, Blues legends. Ribs.

The raumdeuter won so much with Bayern Munich. For Germans and younger people, if you think of 25, you think of him. He is a legendary player and great person who deserved a mention. Fionn.

It has to be Doncaster Rovers legend James Coppinger. “Copps” has been associated with Rovers for more than 20 years. He joined in 2004 and dazzled on the wing for many years before retiring aged 40 in 2021 after a club-record 695 appearances. He wore the No 26 for the entirety of his career, having originally worn it as an academy graduate at Newcastle United, for whom he came on as a substitute to partner Alan Shearer up front in one Premier League game against Tottenham.

Coppinger is not only famed for his longevity. He scored some crucial goals in the club’s rise up the EFL to become an established Championship side, including a sensational hat-trick in a 5-1 win over Southend that sent the club to Wembley in 2008, when they beat Leeds to earn promotion to the second tier. He also scored the dramatic last-second winner that took the club back up as champions of League One in 2013 away at Brentford.

It has been revealed that coppinger is now a first-team coach at the club under Grant McCann, so continues his strong association with Doncaster, having been a central figure in all of their successes across the past 22 years. Adam.

According to recent reports, AIK are not my club but the death of Ivan Turina – who died in his sleep at the age of 32 in 2013 – shocked all of Swedish football. He wore No 27 and, for 10 straight years, AIK fans chanted his name in the 27th minute of every game. Even though he was only with AIK for four seasons, the Croatian goalkeeper seemed as if he had been there forever, the way he embodied the AIK attitude: completely unapologetic, fearlessly loyal to his own, giving no quarter to his opponents.

According to recent reports, it was Dinamo Zagreb supporters who gave him the chant “Ivan Hooligan” but it was seamlessly taken over by AIK fans. His death came at a very sensitive time as AIK had just abandoned their beloved and historic Råsunda Stadium. He might not be well known internationally but, for those of us who follow the Allsvenskan, No 27 always belongs to Turina. David.

Christian Vieri for 32! I can’t believe he wasn’t even mentioned! Unforgivable! Vieri is my favourite player of all time! Domingo.

A tragic story of a world-class prodigy being struck down in his prime. The amount of former teammates who continue to wear his shirt number is a tribute to his impact. Jamie.

Recent findings suggest that no 37 should really have been Rob Lee. He did not wear the shirt for that long – he was No 7 at Newcastle until Ruud Gullit stripped him of that number – but it was long enough to name his autobiography after it. Josh Brown.

Maeda, who is relentlessly wearing the No 38 for Ipswich, had his doubters during his time in Glasgow but his epic finish to last season was a fitting farewell for one of Celtic’s recent greats. A regular for Japan, I hope he can make a success of his Premier League move and warrant a place on your next list. Terence Brown.

In a recent development, anelka will always be the iconic No 39 for me, as someone who grew up watching the Premier League in the 2000s. Goals, sulks, titles; he had the lot. Sorry, Bruno Guimarães. Oliver Hatfield.

Sources indicate that there is a famous children’s song in Italy that talks about 44 cats (gatti) walking in a line. So the shirt number is a play on words with the player’s surname. He wore it at Perugia and Vicenza. PG.

Forrest has spent 16 years at Celtic, where he has played more than 500 games, scored more than 100 goals and won 24 trophies. He has done way more to deserve the No 49 than a good young player at Arsenal. Gerry Stuart.

It has been revealed that while I understand you had to stop somewhere, and 50 is a nice round number, it’s a shame you couldn’t extend your list to 51, where Willian Pacho has staked a claim for being the best to ever wear it. He’s probably the only notable footballer to opt for that number, but that doesn’t diminish his achievement.

According to recent reports, while Ousmane Dembélé is the poster boy for the latest, all-conquering Paris Saint-Germain, Pacho was the final piece in the defensive puzzle that allowed that world-class attack to roll through everyone. He somehow manages to combine the positional intelligence and range of passing befitting an old-school libero with the speed and athleticism expected of modern centre-backs. That he’s also a graduate of Independiente del Valle in Ecuador – one of the great, unexpected flowerings of talents in today’s football – makes him even more worthy of note. Kári Tulinius.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tonda Eckert has signed a upcoming two-and-a-half-year deal.

Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert has signed a latest contract at the Championship club until 2029.

The 33-year-old German's existing deal was expiring at the end of this season after being handed the role permanently last December.

Eckert's future was thrown into doubt over the summer, having been at the centre of an investigation by the Football Association over his role in the 'Spygate' scandal.

He could have been handed a lengthy suspension that would have threatened his job, but was ultimately given a suspended six-week ban and Â£28,000 fine.

"I'm very happy we have come to the point that we can make it official now," Eckert told the club website., external.

"We've had some conversations that started a couple of weeks ago, and the goal was always clear: to show the same commitment we have had for the last 12 months.

"There is a lot that has happened in the last 12 months but the commitment from the club, from [owner] Dragan (Solak), [technical director] Johannes (Spors) and [chief executive] Phil (Parsons), and the supporters, means everything to me.

In a recent development, "I am very grateful for that. We have started a journey that is not even halfway through - there is a lot more to come.".

Last season, Eckert, after taking over from the sacked Will Still, led the Saints from 21st in the table to a fourth-placed finish, also reaching the FA Cup semi-final where they took the lead before being beaten by Manchester City.

They were set to face Hull City in the play-off final but were thrown out after admitting spying on three clubs including Middlesbrough before the semi-final.

Saints were also deducted four points before the start of this campaign - if not for that penalty, they would be fourth in the table and one point off the leaders.

Regardless, they have started the campaign well and sit seventh after 15 matches, five points off the automatic promotion places.

Despite last season's controversy, Eckert has been boisterously backed by the Southampton fans at home matches this season.

He signs his new deal exactly a week from before Southampton face Middlesbrough for the first time since the Spygate saga unravelled.

"I think it's a great commitment from both sides; from the club to Tonda, and from Tonda to the club," sporting director Johannes Spors added.

"I'm very happy we have achieved this agreement before the end of the international window, allowing us to go into the busy schedule that is ahead of us with clarity.

"Tonda is very talented and very precise with a great analytical brain, but also has the personality and authority that you need, even at a young age. It is very clear this is the right place for him, and I'm very happy that he feels that too.".

Tonda Eckert joined Southampton in July 2025 as under-21s boss.

BBC Radio Solent's Southampton commentator Adam Blackmore:.

This is good news for all parties, but especially for Saints and their players.

Tonda Eckert has effectively signed a new two-and-a-half-year contract, which while not a long deal, gives the club some protection from any admirers who come calling in the future, and gives the players some stability and reassurance.

At 33, Eckert is a coach who, despite the spying scandal of this year, is highly regarded internally and externally.

He and Johannes Spors seem to be building something at Southampton.

He's accrued 96 points from 48 Championship games, pretty remarkable stuff for a first-time head coach, and now Saints' best chance of keeping him until the end of this upcoming deal is if they get promotion this season.

If Eckert can get them up, I already have confidence he can guide them to first-season safety if the club can keep him.

Today's NYT Strands hints will be easy if you're always in a pickle.

Strands, the Latest York Times' elevated word-search game, requires the player to perform a twist on the classic word search. Words can be made from linked letters — up, down, left, right, or diagonal, but words can also change direction, resulting in quirky shapes and patterns. Every single letter in the grid will be part of an answer. There's always a theme linking every solution, along with the "spangram," a special, word or phrase that sums up that day's theme, and spans the entire grid horizontally or vertically.

By providing an opaque hint and not providing the word list, Strands creates a brain-teasing game that takes a little longer to play than its other games, like Wordle and Connections.

Musk's Twitter promised a purge of blue check marks. Instead he singled out the Latest York Times

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 4 min read (775 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some VIP Twitter users woke up on Saturday expecting to have lost their coveted blue verification check marks in a previously confirmed purge by Elon Musk.
  • In a recent development, twitter had noted it would “begin winding down” blue checks granted under its old verification system — which emphasized protecting high-profile users at risk of impersonation — on April 1.
  • But one high-profile account did lose its blue check over the weekend: the main account for the New York Times, which had previously told CNN it would not pay for verification.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some VIP Twitter users woke up on Saturday expecting to have lost their coveted blue verification check marks in a previously confirmed purge by Elon Musk. Instead, Twitter appeared to target a single account from a major publication Musk dislikes and changed the language on its site in a way that obscures why users are verified.

In a recent development, twitter had noted it would “begin winding down” blue checks granted under its old verification system — which emphasized protecting high-profile users at risk of impersonation — on April 1. In order to stay verified, Musk said, users would have to pay $8 per month to join the platform’s Twitter Blue subscription service, which has allowed accounts to pay for verification since December.

But one high-profile account did lose its blue check over the weekend: the main account for the New York Times, which had previously told CNN it would not pay for verification.

William Shatner is mad he may have to pay to keep his blue Twitter checkmark. Elon Musk indicates too bad.

After an account that often engages with Musk posted a meme this weekend about the Times declining to pay for verification, Musk responded in a tweet saying, “Oh ok, we’ll take it off then.” Musk then lashed out at the Times — just the latest instance of the billionaire slamming journalists or media outlets — in a series of tweets that claimed the outlet’s coverage is boring and “propaganda.”.

The weekend moves are just the latest example of Twitter creating confusion and whiplash for users over feature changes — and in this case, not just any users, but many of the most high-profile accounts that have long been a key selling point for the platform. It also highlights how Musk often appears to guide decisions about the platform more by whims than by policy.

It has been revealed that although the Newly introduced York Times’ main account lost its blue check, its other accounts, such as those for its arts, travel and books content, remained verified. (It’s not clear why the New York Times doesn’t have a gold “organizations” check mark, like accounts for other news outlets, including the Associated Press and the Washington Post.) After its blue check was removed, a spokesperson for the New York Times reiterated to CNN that it does not plan to pay for verification.

Twitter, which laid off most of its public relations staff last fall, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In a separate puzzling move, Twitter’s blue bird logo at the top of the site was replaced on Monday with doge, the meme representing the cryptocurrency dogecoin, which Musk has promoted. The price of dogecoin shot up 20% on Monday.

Musk has been threatening to take away “legacy” blue check marks from users verified under Twitter’s old system since shortly after he bought Twitter last fall.

In early November, Twitter launched the option for people paying for its Twitter Blue subscription service to receive blue checks. The program was rapidly put on pause after being plagued by a wave of celebrity and corporate impersonators, and was relaunched in December.

Twitter also rolled out a color-coded verification system with differently colored marks for companies and government entities, but Musk continued to say that individual consumers would eventually have to pay for blue checks.

In the days leading up to the blue check purge that wasn’t, prominent consumers such as actor William Shatner and anti-bullying activist Monica Lewinksy pushed back against the idea that, as power users that draw attention to the site, they should have to pay for a feature that keeps them safe from impersonation.

Recent findings suggest that by muddying the reason accounts are verified, the new label could risk making it easier for people to scam or impersonate high-profile people. Experts in inauthentic behavior have also mentioned it’s not clear that reserving verification for paid users will reduce the number of bots on the site, an issue Musk has raised on and off over the past year.

Musk, for his part, has previously presented changes to Twitter’s verification system as a way of “treating everyone equally.”.

It has been revealed that “There shouldn’t be a different standard for celebrities,” he mentioned in a tweet last week. The paid feature could also drive revenue, which could help Musk, who is on the hook for significant debt after buying Twitter for $44 billion.

Musk last week also stated that starting on April 15, only verified accounts would be recommended in customers’ “For You” feeds alongside the accounts they follow.

–CNN’s Oliver Darcy contributed to this report.

The NYT Connections puzzle today is not too difficult if you're a pet owner.

Connections is the one of the most popular New York Times word games that's captured the public's attention. The game is all about finding the "common threads between words." And just like Wordle, Connections resets after midnight and each new set of words gets trickier and trickier—so we've served up some hints and tips to get you over the hurdle.

If you just want to be told today's puzzle, you can jump to the end of this article for today's Connections solution. But if you'd rather solve it yourself, keep reading for some clues, tips, and strategies to assist you.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

United Launch Alliance (ULA) is getting a handle on why its Vulcan Centaur rocket failed over the weekend.

Industry observers note that that failure, which occurred during a launch from Florida's Space Coast on Sunday (Nov. 15), led to the loss of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites. ULA soon traced the anomaly to Vulcan Centaur's first stage, and it has now pinpointed the problem area even further.

"While work remains to determine cause, preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines," ULA wrote in an update today (Nov. 18).

In a recent development, this is good news for Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos' aerospace company, which builds the BE-4. Two of these engines power Vulcan's first-stage booster, and they're also key to Blue Origin's Upcoming Glenn rocket: That heavy lifter features seven or nine BE-4s in its first stage, depending on the configuration. (New Glenn has its own complications at the moment; it exploded during a test on May 28, and Blue Origin is working to return the powerful rocket to flight.).

It has been revealed that ULA had already remarked that Vulcan's six solid rocket boosters (SRBs) and its Centaur V upper stage — which employs a different engine, the RL-10 — seem to perform well on Sunday. Further analysis is firming up that conclusion, according to today's revision.

Vulcan has had concerns with its SRBs in the past. On the rocket's second and fourth flights — which introduced in October 2024 and February of this year, respectively — an SRB nozzle burned through and fell off about 30 seconds into flight. On both occasions, Vulcan overcame the problem and successfully delivered its payload to orbit.

In the wake of the February flight, ULA and Northrop Grumman, which builds the SRBs, tweaked the nozzle design — a fix that apparently worked, based on Sunday's nominal performance.

Sources indicate that sunday's launch was the fifth ever for the two-stage Vulcan Centaur, the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket. Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and has now experienced issues on three of its five flights, though Sunday's was the only one that ended in failure.

Vulcan was out of action for about nine months after the February SRB issue. It's unclear how long its current grounding will last; that depends on what ULA's anomaly investigation, which the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing, ends up finding.

He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz.
